posts.title: C++ Optimizations in MSVC Build Tools 14.52
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
C++ Optimizations in MSVC Build Tools 14.52
The Microsoft C++ team implemented new optimizations in MSVC Build Tools 14.52.
Let’s walk through examples of some of these optimizations. We will focus on
reassociation, loop optimizations, SIMD code generation, inlining, and patterns. Where
noted, we’ll also include a few optimizations that appeared in MSVC 14.51 but
which were not covered in previous blog posts.
Improved Reassociation
We improved arithmetic reassociation to make shared calculations easier to
identify and eliminate. The compiler is free to reassociate integer expressions
and can reassociate floating-point expressions with /fp:fast.
Previously, the compiler reassociated terms that would simplify, such as
x + y - x, and then rebuilt a balanced expression tree. For example:
(((((a + b) + x) + y) - x) + z) => (a + b) + (y + z)

Although this is good, simplification and balancing alone without regard for
common expressions can prevent other optimizations.
Consider this function:
void foo(double x, double y, double z, double d, double* out) {
    out[0] = 1.0 + 2.5 * x * x - d;
    out[1] = 1.0 + 2.5 * y * y - d;
    out[2] = 1.0 + 2.5 * z * z - d;
}

Nothing directly simplifies and there are three addition/subtraction terms so
balancing does not do anything, but all three expressions contain 1.0 - d.
Under /fp:fast, the compiler should arrange for 1.0 - d to occur once:
void foo(double x, double y, double z, double d, double* out) {
    double temp = 1.0 - d;
    out[0] = temp + 2.5 * x * x;
    out[1] = temp + 2.5 * y * y;
    out[2] = temp + 2.5 * z * z;
}

The updated compiler performs this reassociation. It groups subexpressions in a
ranked order where literals come first, followed by loop invariants, then
variants. Grouping invariants next to literals, which are also invariant, helps
the compiler to hoist larger expressions from loops. Within the groups, the
global frequency of each term is considered, including instances where the term
occurs with a different sign. Our algorithm is very similar to the one
described in the global reassociation section of the paper Effective Partial
Redundancy Elimination by Briggs and Cooper.
For example:
void foo2(int n, int x, int* out, int* out2) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        out[i] = 1 + 2 * i + x;
        out2[i] = 1 - 2 * i + x;
    }
}

Applying reassociation, hoisting, and common subexpression elimination yields:
void foo2(int n, int x, int* out, int* out2) {
    int hoisted = 1 + x;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        int temp = 2 * i;
        out[i] = hoisted + temp;
        out2[i] = hoisted - temp;
    }
}

Loop Optimizations
Loop final value optimization
The loop optimizer can replace a repeated induction variable update with a
calculation of its final value. When the intermediate values are not needed
inside the loop, the updates can be removed. If nothing else remains in the
loop, then the loop itself can be removed.
For example, a constant increment repeated a known number of times:
result = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    result += 5;
}

can become:
result = 50;

Other work in the loop does not necessarily prevent final-value optimization.
In this example, printing still requires iteration, but updating result does
not:
result = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    print(i);
    result += 5;
}

The transformed code keeps the printing loop and materializes the result afterward:
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    print(i);
}
result = 50;

A runtime trip count can also be handled:
result = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    result += 5;
}

becomes:
result = n > 0 ? n * 5 : 0;

The zero-trip case is preserved. These transformations assume that the compiler
can establish the conditions needed to preserve the original program’s
behavior.
Better address modes in loops
Address calculations are now optimized with more information about the entire
loop, rather than choosing the largest addressing mode for each instruction in
isolation. The work spans arithmetic-expression reordering, loop-invariant code
motion, common-subexpression elimination, and address-mode construction. The
optimization was motivated by unrolled loops where nearby memory accesses can
share a common base address. It is especially useful on ARM64, where
neighboring loads with a common base can be combined into load-pair (LDP)
instructions. For example, consider this sequence of instructions within a loop:
add x28, x8, #1
add x24, x8, #2
add x27, x8, #3
add x20, x8, #4
add x19, x8, #5
add x15, x8, #6
add x23, x8, #7
add x26, x8, #8
add x22, x8, #9
add x14, x8, #10
add x0, x8, #11
add x13, x8, #12
add x1, x8, #13
add x12, x8, #14
add x7, x8, #15
add x11, x8, #16
add x21, x8, #17
add x25, x8, #18

The loop then used 19 individual indexed loads:
ldr d26, [x10, x28, lsl #3]
ldr d25, [x10, x8, lsl #3]
ldr d23, [x10, x24, lsl #3]
ldr d15, [x10, x27, lsl #3]
ldr d14, [x10, x20, lsl #3]
ldr d13, [x10, x19, lsl #3]
ldr d12, [x10, x15, lsl #3]
ldr d0, [x10, x23, lsl #3]
ldr d1, [x10, x26, lsl #3]
ldr d30, [x10, x22, lsl #3]
ldr d29, [x10, x14, lsl #3]
ldr d2, [x10, x0, lsl #3]
ldr d3, [x10, x13, lsl #3]
ldr d4, [x10, x1, lsl #3]
ldr d28, [x10, x12, lsl #3]
ldr d5, [x10, x7, lsl #3]
ldr d6, [x10, x11, lsl #3]
ldr d7, [x10, x21, lsl #3]
ldr d31, [x10, x25, lsl #3]

The improved code calculates a shared base before the loop:
lsl x24, x8, #3
add x28, x24, x10

The loads in the loop use constant offsets from that base, allowing nine pairs and one remaining individual load:
ldp d25, d26, [x28]
ldp d23, d15, [x28, #16]
ldp d14, d13, [x28, #32]
ldp d12, d0, [x28, #48]
ldp d1, d30, [x28, #64]
ldp d29, d2, [x28, #80]
ldp d3, d4, [x28, #96]
ldp d28, d5, [x28, #112]
ldp d6, d7, [x28, #128]
ldr d31, [x28, #144]

Sharing ARM64 address calculations across indexed accesses
Another address-mode improvement targets accesses that share a fixed member
offset but use different array indices, such as as neighborhood-pattern
computation that loads eight elements from a member array. Each address has the
form:
(basePtr + varyingIndex * elementSize) + memberOffset

Previously, the compiler calculated basePtr + varyingIndex * elementSize
separately for each access and folded memberOffset into the load. Although
each address mode was efficient in isolation, the sequence repeated work.
The improved code instead computes a shared base:
sharedBase = basePtr + memberOffset
address = sharedBase + varyingIndex * elementSize

For example, the old ARM64 sequence contained eight address calculations and
eight loads. The first two accesses looked like this:
add x8, x19, x10, lsl #2
ldr w0, [x8, #0x500]
add x8, x19, x11, lsl #2
ldr w1, [x8, #0x500]

With the member offset included in a shared base, all eight loads can use
scaled-indexed addressing directly:
add x20, x19, #0x500
ldr w0, [x20, x10, lsl #2]
ldr w1, [x20, x11, lsl #2]
ldr w2, [x20, x12, lsl #2]
ldr w3, [x20, x13, lsl #2]
ldr w4, [x20, x14, lsl #2]
ldr w5, [x20, x15, lsl #2]
ldr w6, [x20, x16, lsl #2]
ldr w7, [x20, x17, lsl #2]

This reduces the sequence from 16 instructions to nine. Unlike the preceding
load-pair example, the indices can differ; the opportunity is to share the
fixed part of the address, not to combine adjacent loads.
Hoisting conditionally executed loop-invariant operations
Loop-invariant code motion can now hoist eligible pure operations even when
they originally appeared in a conditional block. The inputs do not change
between iterations, so the calculation need not be repeated whenever the
condition is true.
For example:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (i % 2) {
        sum += a * b;
    }
}

can be transformed into:
c = a * b;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (i % 2) {
        sum += c;
    }
}

The multiplication moves out of the loop and the conditional accumulation stays
in place. This is not a general license to move side effects or unsafe
operations out of conditional execution.
SIMD Code Generation and Vectorization
Small-loop vectorization on ARM64
Starting in MSVC 14.51, the ARM64 loop vectorizer accepts small loops that
exactly fill a vector register, including 64-bit vectors. Previously, a loop
such as this was rejected as too small:
void small_loop(int* __restrict a, const int* __restrict b) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
        a[i] += b[i];
    }
}

Now the loop body vectorizes as:
ldr d17, [x0]
ldr d16, [x1]
add v16.2s, v17.2s, v16.2s
str d16, [x0]

ARM64 NEON bitmask patterns
The first pattern combines negation with a sign test when range information
proves the input to the negation cannot be INT_MIN. For example:
#include <arm_neon.h>

int32x4_t shift_sign_bit_s32(int32x4_t a) {
    return vshrq_n_s32(vnegq_s32(vshrq_n_s32(a, 1)), 31);
}

In MSVC 14.50, the sequence was:
sshr v16.4s, v0.4s, #1
neg v16.4s, v16.4s
cmlt v0.4s, v16.4s, #0

In MSVC 14.51, the initial shift supplies the range information needed to
replace the last two instructions with a positive comparison:
sshr v16.4s, v0.4s, #1
cmgt v0.4s, v16.4s, #0

The second pattern tests whether all bits above the low byte are zero:
#include <arm_neon.h>

int32x4_t test_int32_t(int32x4_t a) {
    return vceqq_s32(vandq_s32(a, vdupq_n_s32(-256)), vdupq_n_s32(0));
}

The literal mask-and-compare implementation in MSVC 14.50:
mvni v16.4s, #0xFF
movi v17.4s, #0
and v16.16b, v0.16b, v16.16b
cmeq v0.4s, v16.4s, v17.4s

is replaced in MSVC 14.51 with an unsigned comparison against 256:
movi v16.4s, #1, lsl #8
cmhi v0.4s, v16.4s, v0.4s

ARM64 NEON pairwise add-and-accumulate patterns
The compiler recognizes a widening pairwise addition followed by accumulation:
#include <arm_neon.h>

uint32x4_t test_uint32x4(uint32x4_t acc, uint16x8_t a) {
    const auto pairs = vpaddlq_u16(a);
    return vaddq_u32(acc, pairs);
}

Instead of the two instructions emitted by MSVC 14.50:
uaddlp v16.4s, v1.8h
add v0.4s, v0.4s, v16.4s

14.51 emits:
uadalp v0.4s, v1.8h

The signed variant similarly uses SADALP.
SLP recognition of scalar reductions
In MSVC 14.51, superword-level parallelism (SLP) vectorization can recognize scalar reductions such as:
int reduce(const int* a) {
    return a[0] + a[1] + a[2] + a[3];
}

ARM64 has a horizontal sum instruction that makes this compact:
ldr q16, [x0]
addv s16, v16.4s

On x64, reducing vector lanes requires a larger sequence. The profitability
decision therefore also considers whether other vectorizable operations can
offset the reduction cost.
SLP recognition of phi nodes
In MSVC 14.52, SLP can vectorize phi nodes, extending its scope beyond straight-line
basic blocks to patterns involving loops. For example, consider two neighboring
accumulations:
#include <stdint.h>

void slp_phi(int64_t* dst, const int64_t* src, int n) {
    int64_t a = 0;
    int64_t b = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i += 2) {
        a += src[i];
        b += src[i + 1];
    }
    dst[0] = a;
    dst[1] = b;
}

These can be processed as two vector lanes. In static single assignment form, phi
nodes merge the initial accumulator values with the values produced by previous
loop iterations. Recognizing those nodes allows SLP to follow the accumulations
through the loop, rather than stopping at the merge.
The transformation can be illustrated with vectorized SSA pseudocode:
a_0 = broadcast(0)
for (i = 0; i < n; i += 2):
    a_1 = phi(a_0, a_2)
    a_2 = a_1 + load(&src[i])
a_3 = phi(a_0, a_2)
store(&dst[0], a_3)

Recognizing adjacent data through address arithmetic
In MSVC 14.52, SLP can recognize more neighboring scalar loads and stores even when
their addresses are written differently. A motivating example accessed pairs of
double values using an index calculated at runtime:
int j = 3 * indices[k];
double dx = xi - x[j];
double dy = yi - x[j + 1];
double r2 = dx * dx + dy * dy;
double scale = 1.0 / (r2 * r2);
double fx = scale * dx;
double fy = scale * dy;
f[j] -= fx;
f[j + 1] -= fy;

To vectorize the neighboring operations, SLP must establish that their memory
accesses are adjacent. For an eight-byte double, it can analyze the second
address as:
x + (j + 1) * 8  ->  x + j * 8 + 8

Both accesses then have the same variable part, x + j * 8, with byte offsets
of zero and eight.
The address builder already supported this distribution when optimizing address
expressions. The change makes it available in analysis-only mode too, so SLP
can record the constant byte offset and prove adjacency without rewriting the
intermediate representation. This applies to both the x loads and the f
updates.
For example, updating the two force components separately on ARM64 requires two
loads, two subtractions, and two stores:
; x0 = &f[j], d0 = fx, d1 = fy
ldr d2, [x0]
ldr d3, [x0, #8]
fsub d2, d2, d0
fsub d3, d3, d1
str d2, [x0]
str d3, [x0, #8]

With both components in a vector register, the update becomes:
; x0 = &f[j], v0.2d = {fx, fy}
ldr q2, [x0]
fsub v2.2d, v2.2d, v0.2d
str q2, [x0]

Optimizing explicit NEON loads and stores
In MSVC 14.52, explicit NEON load and store intrinsics are canonicalized into
generic memory operations. Previously, the compiler kept the specific intrinsics
throughout the optimizer, but they did not match existing optimization patterns
that expected normal loads and stores. Canonicalizing the NEON loads and stores
allowed existing optimizations to apply to them. Ultimately, if the loads and
stores persist after optimization, they may become NEON loads and stores again.
Combining scalar stores when constructing vectors
MSVC 14.52 extends scalar-store combining to more data types and ARM64 NEON.
When scalar assignments construct a vector that is subsequently loaded as a
whole, the compiler can build the value directly in registers rather than
storing each component to the stack and loading it back.
For example:
#include <arm_neon.h>

float32x4_t make_vector(float a, float b, float c, float d) {
    float32x4_t result;
    result.n128_f32[0] = a;
    result.n128_f32[1] = b;
    result.n128_f32[2] = c;
    result.n128_f32[3] = d;
    return result;
}

The register-only construction can use lane inserts:
ins v0.s[1], v1.s[0]
ins v0.s[2], v2.s[0]
ins v0.s[3], v3.s[0]

This small example already stayed in registers in MSVC 14.51. The improvement
is in larger functions, where control flow and register pressure previously
prevented the register allocator from eliminating the temporary stack storage.
Combining the stores earlier also exposes the vector to later SIMD optimizations.
More robust bit-pattern recognition
MSVC 14.52 improves the cost model for recognizing scalar bit-manipulation
patterns when their inputs are defined in another basic block. For example,
this sequence reverses the bits of a 32-bit value:
#include <intrin.h>

unsigned int reverse_bits(unsigned int x) {
    x = ((x & 0x55555555u) << 1) | ((x & 0xAAAAAAAAu) >> 1);
    x = ((x & 0x33333333u) << 2) | ((x & 0xCCCCCCCCu) >> 2);
    x = ((x & 0x0F0F0F0Fu) << 4) | ((x & 0xF0F0F0F0u) >> 4);
    return _byteswap_ulong(x);
}

On ARM64, the calculation can become:
rbit w0, w0

The isolated pattern was already recognized. The new behavior makes recognition
more reliable inside large functions with more complicated control flow.
ARM64 NEON arithmetic with a selected lane
A vector multiplication by a broadcast lane no longer needs a separate
duplicate instruction when the arithmetic instruction can select that lane
directly:
#include <arm_neon.h>

float32x4_t multiply_by_lane(float32x4_t a, float32x4_t b) {
    return vmulq_f32(a, vdupq_laneq_f32(b, 1));
}

MSVC 14.51 emitted:
dup v16.4s, v1.s[1]
fmul v0.4s, v0.4s, v16.4s

MSVC 14.52 folds the broadcast into the multiply:
fmul v0.4s, v0.4s, v1.s[1]

The same recognition applies to fused multiply-add and multiply-subtract,
using the by-element forms of FMLA and FMLS. With /fp:fast, the compiler
can also exchange the multiplicands to expose these forms when the broadcast
appears on the other side of the multiplication.
ARM64 NEON shifted bit-clear patterns
The compiler can combine a mask and shift by moving the mask after the shift
and expressing it as an immediate bit-clear operation:
#include <arm_neon.h>

int32x4_t mask_and_shift(int32x4_t a) {
    return vshlq_n_s32(vandq_s32(a, vdupq_n_s32(2)), 30);
}

Previously, this required loading the mask, applying it, and shifting:
movi v16.4s, #2
and v16.16b, v0.16b, v16.16b
shl v0.4s, v16.4s, #30

MSVC 14.52 instead emits:
shl v0.4s, v0.4s, #30
bic v0.4s, #0x40, lsl #24

The shifted result can contain only bits 30 and 31. Clearing bit 30 leaves
exactly the bit selected by the original mask, without materializing a vector
constant.
Removing masks made redundant by a shift
In related cases, the mask can disappear entirely:
#include <arm_neon.h>

int32x4_t move_low_bit(int32x4_t a) {
    return vshlq_n_s32(vandq_s32(a, vdupq_n_s32(1)), 31);
}

Only the original low bit survives a 31-bit left shift, so masking off the
other bits beforehand does not affect the result. Instead of a MOVI, AND,
and SHL, MSVC 14.52 needs only:
shl v0.4s, v0.4s, #31

Removing work in unused NEON lanes
MSVC 14.52 tracks which vector lanes are observed and can remove instructions
that define only unused lanes. For example, if code inserts zero into lane 3
before an integer vector addition, but subsequently consumes only lanes 0
through 2, the insertion is unnecessary:
; Before
ins v0.s[3], wzr
add v16.4s, v0.4s, v1.4s

; After
add v16.4s, v0.4s, v1.4s

This requires that the remaining operations can safely compute values in the
unused lanes.
The compiler also takes advantage of scalar floating-point and NEON values
sharing the same physical registers. A broadcast is unnecessary if only the
original low lane is used:
#include <arm_neon.h>

float add_low_lane(float a, float b) {
    float32x4_t broadcast = vdupq_n_f32(a);
    return vgetq_lane_f32(broadcast, 0) + b;
}

The previous DUP followed by a scalar addition becomes simply:
fadd s0, s0, s1

ARM64 NEON per-lane rotations
Two complementary shifts combined with a bitwise OR express a rotation within
each vector lane:
#include <arm_neon.h>

uint32x4_t rotate_lanes(uint32x4_t unused, uint32x4_t a) {
    return vorrq_u32(vshrq_n_u32(a, 18), vshlq_n_u32(a, 14));
}

The unused parameter puts a in v1, leaving the return register available
for an instruction that updates its destination. Previously, the calculation
used two shifts and an OR:
shl v17.4s, v1.4s, #14
ushr v16.4s, v1.4s, #18
orr v0.16b, v16.16b, v17.16b

MSVC 14.52 can use unsigned shift-right-and-accumulate:
shl v0.4s, v1.4s, #14
usra v0.4s, v1.4s, #18

The two shifted values occupy disjoint bits, so addition gives the same result
as OR. When both shifts are 16, swapping the two halfwords in each 32-bit lane
performs the whole rotation with one instruction:
rev32 v0.8h, v1.8h

Inlining Improvements
Inlining removes call overhead, but its larger benefit is often exposing
optimizations across a function boundary. MSVC 14.52 improves several decisions
that previously left useful helper functions out of line. The examples below
illustrate the opportunities; they are not minimal reproductions of a missed
inline, and small versions may already inline with earlier compilers.
Single-call-site helpers inside force-inline functions
The inliner can give special consideration to eligible functions with a single
call site. Previously, this analysis was disabled while optimizing a
__forceinline root function, even when its helper was explicitly marked
inline.
Consider this call structure:
static inline unsigned mix(unsigned x) {
    x ^= x >> 16;
    x *= 0x7FEB352Du;
    x ^= x >> 15;
    return x;
}

__forceinline unsigned bucket(unsigned x) {
    return mix(x) & 255u;
}

unsigned lookup_bucket(unsigned x) {
    return bucket(x);
}

The __forceinline on bucket does not itself request that mix be inlined.
The improvement allows the single-call-site heuristic to consider a
user-marked inline helper such as mix while optimizing bucket.
The result can expose the helper’s arithmetic together with its caller’s
masking and other surrounding work.
Keeping slightly larger small helpers inline
MSVC 14.52 raises the small-function allowance from 40 to 50 instructions. The
motivating NEON shuffle helpers were roughly 48 nodes, just outside the old
allowance.
For example, a SIMD abstraction can wrap lane selection in a template:
#include <arm_neon.h>

template<int Lane>
inline float32x4_t broadcast_lane(float32x4_t value) {
    return vdupq_laneq_f32(value, Lane);
}

float32x4_t scale_vector(float32x4_t a, float32x4_t b) {
    return vmulq_f32(a, broadcast_lane<1>(b));
}

Keeping such wrappers inline exposes the constant lane selection to the SIMD
optimizer, allowing opportunities such as the by-element multiply described
above. The example is deliberately small; the allowance change matters for
larger wrappers whose intermediate representation falls between the old and
new limits. These are compiler-internal size estimates, not source-line counts
or a new unconditional inlining guarantee.
Accounting for scalar replacement of local aggregates
The inliner now recognizes more calls whose removal can enable scalar
replacement of aggregates (SROA) and dead-store elimination. Passing the address
of a local struct to a function forces it to have a memory location, such
that the entire struct is written to memory in the caller. The called function
might use only a few fields of the struct. Inlining exposes the fields that
are actually needed, allowing the optimizer to keep those useful values in
registers and skip copying the struct to memory.
For example:
#include <stdint.h>

struct Values {
    uint64_t a, b, c, d;
};

void adjust(Values* values, uint64_t delta) {
    values->a += delta;
    values->b += delta;
    values->c += delta;
    values->d += delta;
}

uint64_t calculate(
    uint64_t a, uint64_t c, uint64_t delta) {
    Values values = {a, 0, c, 0};
    adjust(&values, delta);
    return values.a + values.c;
}

Once adjust is inlined, the struct and the updates to its unused b and
d fields can disappear. The useful calculation is equivalent to:
return (a + delta) + (c + delta);

The new heuristic gives a bonus to eligible calls that the normal
heuristic would otherwise decline. It combines a summary of the
callee’s fixed-offset pointer accesses with caller-side evidence that the
argument is a suitable local aggregate. Pointer escapes, variable-offset
accesses, and other cases the analysis cannot safely characterize do not
receive this benefit.
Pattern-based Optimizations
MSVC 14.52 recognizes additional profitable arithmetic, selection, comparison,
and bitwise-expression patterns. The examples in this section use simplified
x64 assembly for optimized builds with /O2; the reciprocal transformation
additionally requires /fp:fast.
Sharing a reciprocal across repeated divisions
Several divisions by the same floating-point value can share a reciprocal:
void divide_by_common_value(
    double a, double b, double c, double divisor, double* out) {
    out[0] = a / divisor;
    out[1] = b / divisor;
    out[2] = c / divisor;
}

Instead of three separate divisions:
divsd xmm0, xmm3
divsd xmm1, xmm3
divsd xmm2, xmm3

the compiler can perform one division followed by three multiplications:
movsd xmm4, QWORD PTR [one]
divsd xmm4, xmm3
mulsd xmm0, xmm4
mulsd xmm1, xmm4
mulsd xmm2, xmm4

This transformation requires /fp:fast. It is cost-based rather than
unconditional: with only a few uses, direct division may be preferable because
introducing a reciprocal adds a temporary and can lengthen live ranges.
More branchless selections on x64
The x64 if-conversion profitability decision now accepts nonzero integer
constants in a pattern already supported on ARM64. A small selection such as:
int select_value(int a, int b) {
    return a < b ? a + b : 7;
}

might previously use a branch:
lea eax, DWORD PTR [rcx+rdx]
cmp ecx, edx
jl selected_sum
mov eax, 7
selected_sum:

In MSVC 14.52, it instead can select between register values with a conditional move:
cmp ecx, edx
lea eax, DWORD PTR [rcx+rdx]
mov r8d, 7
cmovge eax, r8d

This removes the control-flow branch and its potential misprediction cost.
Collapsing Boolean expressions to XOR
Some multi-operation Boolean expressions compute a simple exclusive OR:
unsigned symmetric_difference(unsigned a, unsigned b) {
    return (a | b) & ~(a & b);
}

A literal implementation might use:
mov eax, ecx
or ecx, edx
and eax, edx
not eax
and eax, ecx

Recognizing the identity reduces the sequence to:
xor ecx, edx
mov eax, ecx

Related forms, including XOR combinations of the AND and OR of the same
operands, can simplify in the same way.
Reusing equivalent reversed comparisons
Reversing both comparison operands and the condition can express the same test.
Recognizing that equivalence avoids computing identical Boolean values
independently:
int equivalent_compare_difference(int a, int b) {
    const int first = a >= b ? 1 : 0;
    const int second = b <= a ? 1 : 0;
    return first - second;
}

Instead of:
xor r8d, r8d
cmp edx, ecx
setle r8b
xor eax, eax
cmp ecx, edx
setge al
sub eax, r8d

the entire expression becomes:
xor eax, eax

Canonicalizing the comparison both enables reuse and exposes the constant result of subtracting equal values.
Recognizing equivalent minimum and maximum selections
Two differently written selections can also compute the same minimum or maximum:
int equivalent_max_difference(int a, int b) {
    const int first = a > b ? a : b;
    const int second = b > a ? b : a;
    return first - second;
}

Without recognizing their equivalence, the compiler might emit:
cmp edx, ecx
mov eax, ecx
cmovg eax, edx
cmovl edx, ecx
sub edx, eax
mov eax, edx

Both selections return the same value, so the optimized result is simply:
xor eax, eax

The recognition covers signed minimum and maximum forms with strict or
non-strict comparisons, including equivalent results combined with XOR. Besides
saving instructions directly, these simplifications reduce temporary values and
can expose further opportunities in later optimization passes.
Conclusion
The Microsoft C++ team released many new optimizations in MSVC Build Tools
14.52. We will continue focusing on performance while developing MSVC 14.53.
Many thanks to the compiler engineers who implemented the optimizations and
helped write sections of this blog post, including Alex Wong, Aman Arora,
Chris Pulido, Reka Kovacs, and Swaroop Sridhar.
MSVC Build Tools 14.52 is available as part of Visual Studio 2026.
Try it out today and share your feedback on Visual Studio Developer Community.

posts.title: MSVC Build Tools version 14.52 now generally available
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Microsoft C++ (MSVC) Build Tools version 14.52 is now generally available as a long-term support (LTS) release. It is available with Visual Studio 2026 version 18.12 on the Stable Channel and Visual Studio 2026 LTSC version 18.11, both released on November 10.
With this release, C++23 is ready for production use through /std:c++23, and the Standard Library is C++23 feature complete. You also get code-generation improvements for x64 and ARM64 and the general availability of C++ Dynamic Debugging.
An LTS toolset for your team
MSVC 14.52 gives teams that want to standardize on a C++ toolset an LTS option in both Visual Studio channels. Stable continues to receive Visual Studio feature and quality updates; LTSC is an option if your organization wants to limit changes to its Visual Studio environment. Learn more in Announcing Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11.
MSVC and Visual Studio have their own support lifecycles. Keep your Visual Studio installation and MSVC toolset current with applicable servicing updates. This release was not scheduled to be an LTS under our current lifecycle, but we added 14.52 as LTS to help C++ workload teams upgrade and stay in sync with VS. We’ll share more about the MSVC lifecycle in a future announcement.
What’s new in MSVC 14.52
The MSVC Build Tools Preview updates – August 2026 post covered work targeting 14.52 across the compiler, optimizer, linker, Standard Library, and related tools. The later 14.52 Release Candidate post has the full change list. Here are a few highlights:
C++23 for production: /std:c++23 is now available. The STL is C++23 feature complete; constexpr <cmath> and <cstdlib> support is opt-in with /Zc:cmath. See the STL Changelog and constexpr cmath with LLVM libc.
Better optimization across architectures: The preview updates added improvements to inlining, loop optimization, vectorization, and instruction selection. ARM64 benefits include better vector operations and load pairing; x64 gains include expanded APX code generation.
APX targeting now generally available: MSVC 14.52 brings production support for targeting Intel Advanced Performance Extensions (APX) in x64 builds.
More reliable C++ modules and diagnostics: 14.52 greatly improves the reliability of C++ modules with updates to diagnostics, dependent code scenarios, and better feedback at link time.
Libraries and tools: Highlights include SVE-vectorized Standard Library algorithms on ARM64, improved AddressSanitizer performance and instruction decoding, and better handling of large debug-information streams.
C++ Dynamic Debugging: Now generally available with MSVC 14.52, making it easier to inspect optimized builds.
Community fixes: The preview and RC posts list many fixes reported through Developer Community, including compiler, code-generation, C++ modules, linker, and library issues.
Update with confidence
Step 1 – Install or update Visual Studio 2026 and MSVC
Use the Visual Studio Installer to install or update Visual Studio 2026 18.12 on Stable or Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11. Select the C++ workload and the MSVC 14.52 components for the architectures you need.
Step 2 – Configure your projects
Load your project in Visual Studio 2026. If you are using CMake, check that your configuration selects MSVC 14.52. If you are using MSBuild (.vcxproj) and moving from an MSVC version that came with Visual Studio 2022 or earlier, the Setup Assistant helps you retarget your projects. To open it manually, select Project > Retarget solution. You can also update the Platform Toolset in the project property pages.
Step 3 – Use GitHub Copilot modernization for C++ to resolve upgrade issues quickly
Use the @Modernize agent in the GitHub Copilot Chat window in Visual Studio to speed up your move to MSVC 14.52. It inspects your build for upgrade-related issues and works with you to resolve them, possibly saving hours or days. Learn more about upgrading MSVC with the @Modernize agent on Microsoft Learn.
MSVC Build Tools Previews
To try work in progress, install Visual Studio 2026 Insiders and select the MSVC Build Tools Preview. Insiders receives preview updates more frequently. Previews are not serviced; for a supported, long-lived baseline, use 14.52.
Update today!
MSVC 14.52 combines C++23 for production, improved generated code and a long-term support option. Update today and share your feedback on Visual Studio Developer Community.

posts.title: MSVC Build Tools Preview updates – November 2026
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
The MSVC Build Tools Preview is updated regularly with the latest features and fixes from the MSVC development team. This post covers the last month’s updates of the Preview build tools, currently targeting the v14.53 release. This encompasses changes across the compiler frontend, backend, linker, standard library, and related tools.
Although you can acquire the MSVC Build Tools Preview through either the Visual Studio 2026 Stable Channel or Visual Studio 2026 Insiders Channel , Insiders gets MSVC Preview updates more frequently.
To check if it’s installed simply make sure one or both of these components are checked in the installer:
MSVC Build Tools for x64/x86 (Preview)
MSVC Build Tools for ARM64/ARM64EC (Preview)
Follow the instructions on https://aka.ms/msvc/preview to configure your IDE & command prompts to use the MSVC Build Tools Preview.
The version number printed by cl.exe and link.exe will be at least 19.53.36930 / 14.53.36930.
We appreciate any feedback that you may have. Please report any issues on Visual Studio Developer Community so we can address them by the time we move out of preview.
C++ Conformance and Frontend
Added support for [[fallthrough]] in C++14 mode.
Added C++ warnings C4878 and C4879 for additional explicit and implicit conversions between HRESULT or SCODE and Boolean-like types. Both warnings are level 4 and off by default. Ticket
Added /Zc:__super[-] and /Zc:__if_exists[-] to control the __super and __if_exists Microsoft extensions.
Reduced frontend memory usage by improving allocation and lifetime management for buffered source tokens.
Added -fsanitize-coverage-ignorelist as an alternative spelling for -fsanitize-coverage-blocklist, preserving compatibility with existing command lines. Ticket
Code Generation and Optimization
ARM64 improvements:
Extended experimental support for the Arm Scalable Matrix Extension under /feature:sme, including streaming-function declarations, supported direct and indirect calls, link-time code generation, exception handling, and runtime state-management helpers. Support is native ARM64 only and remains partial; streaming-function definitions and ARM64EC are not supported.
Added the ARM64_FPMR constant for _ReadStatusReg and _WriteStatusReg, along with the FPMR register name in the ARM64 assembler and disassembler. Executing these instructions requires hardware and operating-system support.
Improved inlining decisions on ARM64 and ARM64EC by accounting for floating-point and vector-register pressure, helping avoid unnecessary spills.
Replaced some multi-step NEON zero-extension sequences with a table-lookup instruction.
x64 and x86 improvements:
Expanded APX conditional-compare generation, including comparisons produced when lowering switch statements, and improved conditional-move instruction selection.
Re-enabled compact x64 epilog generation for unwind version 3.
Improved AVX-512 instruction selection by combining supported arithmetic-and-blend sequences into merge-masked arithmetic instructions.
Replaced eligible late-stage constant multiplications on x64 with shorter address-calculation instructions.
Optimizer improvements:
Added opt-in automatic load-time function selection for link-time code generation. The [[msvc::auto_dispatch]] attribute can generate CPU-specific implementations from one function body for selection by a supporting loader.
Improved inlining decisions to expose more opportunities for simplifying aggregate objects and eliminating unused stores.
Improved constant-remainder optimization on x86 and ARM64, replacing eligible hardware divisions with multiply-and-shift sequences.
Removed redundant comparisons and unreachable branches inside loops when their outcomes follow from the loop bounds.
Expanded vectorization opportunities by recognizing more non-overlapping memory accesses and more ways to pack scalar values into vectors.
Added partial support for vectorizing groups of three elements.
Improved loop-unswitching decisions so more loops can be simplified before vectorization, including eligible conditions read through pointers.
Reduced padding in generated runtime type information and exception-handling data, helping reduce 64-bit executable and DLL sizes.
Linker and Assembler
Added the opt-in linker option /WARNUNUSEDLIBS. It emits LNK4324 for each input library from which no members were loaded. The warning supports /IGNORE:4324 and warning-as-error settings without changing /VERBOSE:UNUSEDLIBS. Ticket
Improved incremental-link performance for projects with large numbers of input files by reducing repeated filename searches.
Expanded the set of valid epilog instructions accepted by MASM with unwind version 3, including VERW and SWAPGS.
Static Analysis
Expanded C26433 and C26435 checking to virtual destructor overrides, aligning the checks with the current C++ Core Guidelines. Ticket
AddressSanitizer
Added the opt-in windows_shadow_top_down option on 64-bit Windows. Setting ASAN_OPTIONS=windows_shadow_top_down=1 before AddressSanitizer initializes places shadow memory in the highest available address range that fits, rather than the lowest. This can reduce managed-runtime memory overhead when loading an instrumented DLL into an application using the .NET Framework garbage collector. The option is off by default, has no effect on 32-bit Windows, and must be set through the environment early enough to affect initialization; __asan_default_options is too late to change shadow placement.
Standard Library
See the STL changelog for details on standard library improvements in the MSVC Build Tools Preview.
Tickets Fixed
The following tickets reported through Developer Community have been fixed in this update:
_Pragma in header unit causes ICE with preview platform toolset 19.52.36725
/EHa compiler 19.52preview optimizes away local variable accessed from catch block
/Zc:checkGwOdr fails to detect ODR violations when used with /GL
&Derived::f as an argument of an auto non-type template parameter gets a malformed type when f comes from a using-declaration
[[msvc::dispatch]]: nested all() inside any() is flattened
<ranges> plus import std triggers C2382
14.52: C1001 “Internal Compiler Error” on ARM64 when compiling /GL + /LTCG

Adding a zero vector incorrectly preserves negative zero

ADL fails to consider the namespace associated with the base class under a specific scenario

ARM64 /GL + /LTCG: wrong vector-move code in cmsofflineservicing.dll (MSVC 19.52)

posts.title: C++ Dynamic Debugging is now generally available
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Introduction
We are excited to announce that C++ Dynamic Debugging is now generally available in all Visual Studio 2026 channels and the Microsoft C++ (MSVC) Build Tools version 14.52.
In the traditional workflow for games or large applications, switching to a debug build gives you access to debug symbols at the expense of performance. In contrast, when you debug optimized or release builds, you’ll often encounter variables that are “optimized away” and find it difficult to step reliably through the code you want to inspect.
With C++ Dynamic Debugging, you get the best of both worlds. You can inspect local variables, step through your source line by line, and step into inlined functions. The rest of your application stays optimized, so you can keep the runtime performance you need to reach and investigate a problem.
After turning on the feature and rebuilding your application, Dynamic Debugging will deoptimize functions for you when setting a breakpoint or stepping into a function. You don’t need to stop, add #pragma optimize, rebuild, and reproduce the issue again just to inspect that code. For large games and performance-sensitive applications, that means less time preparing to debug and more time investigating the issue.
Before (Optimized)
After (With C++ Dynamic Debugging)
Customer Feedback
From game development to virtual reality, Microsoft teams have already been using C++ Dynamic Debugging to make optimized code easier to debug. Here’s what they’re saying:
“Dynamic Debugging is a game changer for C++ development. It lets me work in the optimized builds I actually need for large game codebases, while still being able to deoptimize and inspect code and runtime state when it matters. It removes a longstanding tradeoff between realistic runtime performance and a productive debugging experience.”
Michael Buschbeck – Principal Software Engineer, Microsoft Havok
“Performance is critical when developing virtual reality applications, so my team builds with optimizations on. Dynamic Debugging lets us debug that optimized code as if it were unoptimized. It’s so seamless you forget how much it’s helping.”
Bryce Hutchings – Principal Software Engineer, Microsoft Cloud Streaming, Mixed Reality, and Graphics

Try it in your project
For an x64 MSBuild C++ project, select your Release configuration then open project properties. Set Configuration Properties > Advanced > Use C++ Dynamic Debugging > Yes. Then, rebuild your project to get started. This setting turns off Whole Program Optimization. For CMake and other build systems, you can pass the new /dynamicdeopt switch to cl.exe, lib.exe, and link.exe.
C++ Dynamic Debugging also works with Unreal Engine 5.6 and later, with support in Unreal Build Tool and Unreal Build Accelerator. To try it, enable WindowsPlatform.bDynamicDebugging = true; in your target’s .Target.cs file and rebuild.
In addition, Dynamic Debugging is compatible with distributed build systems like FastBuild and IncrediBuild.
See the documentation for other build systems, requirements, and limitations.
Share your feedback
We would love to hear how C++ Dynamic Debugging works for your projects. Share your thoughts by commenting below, through Help > Send Feedback in Visual Studio, on X (@VisualC), or by email at visualcpp@microsoft.com.

posts.title: How Meta Uses AI Agents to Scale ML Innovations Across Ads Ranking Models
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Our previous post in this series introduced the Ranking Engineer Agent (REA), an autonomous system that generates hypotheses, designs experiments, and proves new machine learning (ML) techniques on ads ranking models. 
Now, we’re sharing how we propagate ranking model improvements like architectural advancements and training optimizations efficiently across a large and diverse fleet of ads ranking models.  
This post walks through this process that we call “technique propagation” and how we’re optimizing the process using AI agents.
Since agents began driving execution in March 2026, we estimate AI agents handle over 60% of all technique propagation. Measured against the same work before agents, early results show 3x greater engineering productivity, a median 4x reduction in training compute across select combinations, and an estimated $45M+ in compute savings by the end of the year.
Meta’s ads recommendation system is powered by a large number of distinct ads ranking models, each serving different product surfaces and advertiser objectives, and each with its own architecture, training data, and serving constraints. 
Across this portfolio, ML researchers and engineers are continuously advancing the state-of-the-art through innovations we call “techniques.” A technique is anything that makes a ranking model better such as architectural advancements like Wukong factorization layers, Interformer interaction networks, richer data representations, training optimizations, or efficiency improvements in training and inference.
However, because each model has its own architecture, data, and training and serving constraints, a technique proven on one model almost never copy-pastes onto the next. At the same time, speed matters because ML techniques have a shelf life. An innovation that delivers gains today may be superseded within a couple of model development cycles. The faster proven techniques reach the full model fleet, the more value they deliver before the next generation of techniques arrive.
So how do we propagate a technique to a diverse fleet of models as quickly as possible, while minimizing engineering bandwidth and compute? 
Scaling Technique Propagation
Propagating a growing inventory of proven techniques across a large fleet of diverse models creates a combinatorially expanding space of technique-model combinations to explore, where both engineering bandwidth and compute become significant constraints.
The standard way to adapt a technique is to have engineers who are domain experts manually execute adaptation. An engineer studies how a technique interacts with a specific model’s architecture, generalizes it, and tunes it to that model’s constraints. This produces the strongest results, and is still the process for our highest-revenue models, but it does not scale to all of the models in the space. Each adaptation is effort-intensive and demands deep familiarity with both the technique and the target model. So throughput is capped by engineering bandwidth while the opportunity for adaptation grows much faster.
The second constraint on propagation is compute. Every adaptation attempt requires a training run, and with a finite compute budget the question is not only which techniques to try but how to navigate the combinatorial space of configurations without spending the budget on attempts (most of which will produce suboptimal gains). 
Both constraints point to the same requirement: To propagate techniques to a large number of diverse models quickly, propagation has to become standardized, automated, and able to make judgment calls. 
We started by standardizing model design and automating propagation: a template-driven approach organizes models into a small set of reusable and composable building blocks, so a technique validated once at the template level propagates automatically to every model built from that template. Over the last 2 years, through standardization and automation, we have shipped 5,000+ technique-model combinations across our large, diverse fleet of models while reducing per-model engineering time by 92%. You can read more about it in our post on Standard Model Templates (SMT).
Standardization and automation handle the deterministic steps, but successful and efficient propagation still requires making judgment calls, such as which technique is worth propagating to which model, how wide a hyperparameter search should be, why a model is not showing gains, or how to detect and resolve failures. Those decisions still required significant human bandwidth, which prevented us from scaling further and from reaching a state where all techniques reached all applicable models within a few weeks of being proven.
That is where AI agents come in.
Scaling Technique Propagation With AI Agents

Our technique propagation system is built around three capabilities:
Discovery: Keep a live view of which techniques have been proven and estimate how well each might transfer to generate a prioritized set of technique-model candidates, ranked by expected impact.
Generalization: Generalize a proven technique so it works on models it was not originally designed for. For models built from shared templates, a technique is generalized once per template and reaches every model built from it. Beyond what templates cover, each model needs its own adaptation, which is where the deepest technical reasoning happens.
Adoption: Turn validated adaptations into shipped models, many at a time: launching experiments, managing asynchronous multi-day training runs, monitoring convergence, diagnosing and recovering from failures, and assembling proposals that can land.
Today, AI agents supercharge all the above capabilities by taking on the judgment-heavy, non-deterministic decision making and bringing deep intelligence to the system. They combine LLM-based reasoning with specialized ML tooling to handle the work of deciding which adaptations to try, diagnosing why something failed and automatically mitigating it, navigating hyperparameter search spaces efficiently, and managing capacity across hundreds of concurrent jobs. The agents share a common knowledge base, an accumulated record of prior training runs, model architectures, and technique outcomes, so they build on what has already been learned rather than starting from scratch.

How Agents Speed Up Discovery
Discovery answers two questions: What proven techniques exist, and how applicable are they to each model in the model fleet? Until recently, domain experts answered both, working through the assessments one model at a time. They tracked research and results across the organization, spotted the techniques worth propagating, and relied on their domain knowledge to judge applicability.
Agents aren’t constrained by the same knowledge or engineering bandwidth limitations as domain experts. Instead of relying on what any one expert knows, they draw on the shared knowledge base, and they make assessments across the entire model fleet at once rather than one model at a time. They systematically identify which proven techniques exist, estimate their transferability across the model fleet, and produce prioritized technique lists ranked by expected impact. Engineers now only have to review the agents’ assessments and make a decision from there.
How Agents Make Generalization More Computationally Efficient 
Generalization is the process of re-implementing a technique proven on one model so it applies to models with different architectures, feature representations, training data, and serving constraints. The core idea usually transfers, but the implementation almost never does. The customization needed depends on the technique and the target model, ranging from retuning hyperparameters, to adapting features to what the target model already consumes or resizing the architecture to fit its inference budget, to redesigning the technique outright. Deciding what a given model needs, and how far to go, is a judgment call.
Depending on whether a model is built from standardized templates or customized individually, generalization comes in two flavors, and agents assist with both:
Template generalization: For models built from standardized templates, agents assist with building, evaluating, and improving the templates themselves. They propose template optimization hypotheses from proven techniques, launch experiments across representative model sets, evaluate results, diagnose failures, and iterate through multiple rounds, helping manage the multi-day loops that template development requires. Validating a technique once at the template level costs a fraction of the compute of adapting each model separately.
Bespoke generalization: For our highest-revenue models, where we still customize a technique for each model, agents progressively learn while working alongside ML engineers during the initial application of a technique to a small number of models. As the engineer makes adaptation decisions such as adjusting configurations, tuning hyperparameters, or resolving failures, the agent tracks every change and outcome, encoding what works, what doesn’t, and which decisions are model-specific versus generalizable. With that grounding, the agent proposes and tests adaptations for the remaining models, with the engineer reviewing and steering rather than driving each one.
Drawing on millions of prior training runs and each target model’s own properties, agents start from the configurations most likely to work, use the results of each round of training runs to narrow the hyperparameter search space for the next, and decide which experiments are worth continuing and which to stop early. As a result, when measured across select technique-model combinations, we have seen a median 4x reduction in training compute.
How Agents Accelerate Adoption
At the adoption stage, agents ship generalized techniques model-by-model. They launch experiments, manage asynchronous multi-day training runs, fine-tune each model, monitor convergence, recover from failures, and assemble validated proposals.
Fine-tuning happens differently depending on how the technique arrived. For techniques applied individually, agents help find the best configuration of technique bundles for that particular model. For models built from a shared template, an auto-research loop searches on top of the template, tuning each model for the gains the shared configuration alone does not deliver.
When failures occur, whether from an infrastructure issue, training divergence, or a data pipeline error, integrated debugging and recovery diagnose the root cause and apply targeted fixes or retries. 
Running hundreds of these workflows at once raises the question of which jobs get priority, and which runs are worth continuing or stopping early. Getting the most out of a fixed compute budget is a global optimization problem, and it is where we are currently investing. Agents monitor concurrent training jobs, rank them by revenue importance, technique potential, and deadline proximity, and reclaim capacity from stalled or low-value runs, so GPUs stay pointed at the highest-value work rather than sitting idle or queued behind lower-priority experiments.
In the past, an engineer had to watch each run, triage every failure by hand, and restart it, which capped each of them at a handful of models. Now they can keep oversight at the decision points, approving plans and setting priorities at a 3x greater productivity (each engineer can now handle 3x more technique-model adaptations), compressing the time from a proven technique to a shipped model.
How We Evaluate Agent-Driven Propagation
Techniques propagated by agents are evaluated the same way as those propagated by engineers. A technique has to show improved offline metrics for predictive performance, such as normalized entropy (NE), while not regressing on key guardrails like training or inference cost. It then has to show a statistically significant win in online A/B testing before it can be shipped.
But a single evaluation at the end comes too late to steer an agent working across stages over days. Each stage produces a different artifact, so each needs its own metrics. This is how we validate what agents are doing.
Discovery: We measure the precision and recall of the technique-model candidates agents select. For a given technique, precision is the share of selected models where the technique ultimately ships, and recall is the share of all viable models for that technique that agents surfaced. Recall matters more here, since a model missed at this stage never gets a second chance; precision acts as a guardrail against spending compute on techniques that will not work.
Generalization: We evaluate techniques generalized by agents across a wide range of models to ensure each delivers gains beyond the model it was originally proven on. We first test every generalized technique on scaled-down versions of models, screening technique-model adaptations broadly while keeping compute usage efficient. Then techniques that pass are evaluated on a representative set of full-size models, where they must improve NE and meet every guardrail metric before moving to adoption.
Adoption: At this stage, we continue to evaluate correctness with the same predictive performance and guardrail metrics as before. But adoption is also the most operationally heavy stage, with experiments that run for days, so we evaluate agent productivity as well. Two metrics matter most: the number of human interventions needed to complete an experiment, which shows how much engineering time each experiment still takes, and the percentage of issues agents diagnose and mitigate on their own.
Humans continue to be key stakeholders throughout the propagation process, reviewing key decisions, confirming judgment calls, and ultimately approving what ships.
Making Agent-Driven Propagation the Standard at Meta 
Given our early results, we are ramping agent-driven workflows to be the primary modality for technique propagation across the model fleet.
Today it can take over a year for every proven technique to reach every applicable model. We’re aiming to reduce that time down to three months. Achieving that means pushing agent-driven workflows toward 5x higher end-to-end throughput, so propagation keeps pace with innovation rather than trailing it. 
To get there we are continuing to invest in the intelligence of the agents themselves, improving the quality of generalization, capacity efficiency, and execution through self-evolving learning, where agents refine their own strategies based on accumulated outcomes rather than relying solely on human-provided heuristics.
Propagating techniques across the models is one component of a larger vision. We are agentifying every aspect of the end-to-end model development lifecycle across the ranking AI space, from exploration and hypothesis generation to propagation, experimentation, and production launch. These agents represent the scaling layer of this system, ensuring that every proven innovation reaches its full potential across the model fleet.

posts.title: Design Once, Deploy at Scale: Building a Template-Driven ML Ecosystem
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
As ML ecosystems grow to a large number of production models, the bottleneck is no longer inventing new techniques to improve these models, but rather shipping them reliably and efficiently across a fragmented model space, creating a rising tide that lifts all the boats.
At Meta, we built a template-driven approach that standardizes model design into a small set of reusable and composable building blocks, turning model iteration from a per-model problem into a shared systems problem.
Over the last two years, this approach reduced per-model engineering time by 92%, shipped 5000+ technique-model combinations, improved offline model quality by 0.63% on average at neutral serving capacity, and delivered 0.86% cumulative online lift covering 70% of models by count.
This work is fully detailed in our paper, “Design Once, Deploy at Scale: Template-Driven ML Development for Large Model Ecosystems.”
Meta’s ads ranking systems process billions of daily requests across a diverse array of products and optimization goals, served by a large number of production models. At that scale, the main challenge in improving user relevance and advertiser value has shifted from inventing new techniques to propagating them. Every high-impact idea needs to reach every model it applies to, and adapting it one model at a time does not scale with the fleet.
Fragmentation compounds quickly in large-scale ML systems. A new architecture lands on one model, but bringing it to every corner of the ecosystem may take years. A platform migration works for one family of models, but breaks on a long tail of specialized configurations. A tuning insight improves one model, but says little about the next one because the underlying setup is too different. Over time, propagation becomes more difficult than the innovation itself.
Meta’s ads ranking ecosystem ran into this exact problem. As the number of production models grew with the diversity of ads optimization objectives, so did the diversity of architectures, features, training settings, serving constraints, and platform-specific logic. That diversity gave teams flexibility, but it also created three systemic problems: high engineering cost to ship new ideas broadly, high reliability cost from an explosion of corner cases, and low predictability when trying to estimate the ecosystem-wide impact of a change.
The deeper issue is that fragmentation creates an unfavorable scaling law for engineering itself. If each idea must be evaluated and adapted per model, the work grows linearly with the number of models. That is manageable early on, but becomes a serious bottleneck when you have a large number of models. 
Fragmentation also weakens automation. AutoML and optimization systems work best in a structured space, but when every model has a different shape, the highest-potential techniques reach only a subset of models.
Our answer was not to add another layer of automation on top of this complexity. Instead, we started by reducing the complexity itself. We did this by introducing Standard Model Templates (SMT), an approach that standardizes model design into a curated set of reusable templates.
Figure 1: Before SMT, each technique was tuned by hand on each model, and the combinations to try grew exponentially. With SMT, multi-model optimization tunes techniques once across representative models, and the ones that generalize go into the next template version.
A Template-Driven Foundation
A template is an opinionated, minimal model setup built from shared components such as architecture choices, feature logic, training settings, and serving configs. Instead of maintaining every production model as a largely independent design, we group similar models around a smaller number of standard templates. Model-specific logic still exists where necessary, but the common parts are explicitly represented and shared.
In practice, we use a small set of templates that cover major ranking and retrieval patterns across different model sizes. These templates package reusable components for feature selection, feature interaction, model parallelism, training configuration, and hardware-aware serving.
This changes the operating model in an important way. Instead of evaluating a new idea independently on every model, we can evaluate it on a much smaller set of representative templates and then propagate it to the model groups that use them. In other words, we shift from per-model iteration to template-level iteration.
That gives us three main advantages.
Reduced propagation complexity: A shared template lets one implementation serve many downstream models, which lowers the cost of shipping new ideas at scale.
Improved reliability: When there are fewer unique model setups, it becomes practical to build stronger validation, better guardrails, and more transferable debugging workflows. Problems such as training instability or serving regressions become easier to reason about because they occur within a shared template structure rather than an unbounded configuration space.
Improved predictability: When models in a group share a common template, performance on representative models becomes a much better signal for the rest of the group. That makes ecosystem-level planning more grounded and less assumption-driven.
Over time, this template-driven approach became more than a standardization effort. It became the foundation for a broader ML development system.
Figure 2: The SMT development loop (left) and the layered architecture inside each template (right). Techniques are tuned once across representative models, added to a new template version, and rolled out to every model built on it.
SMTs: From Standardization to Scalable Technique Transfer
The shift to SMTs unlocked a more ambitious capability — the ability to optimize the entire ecosystem as a single, cohesive unit. Rather than managing a fleet of independent models, we began treating the landscape as a shared innovation surface.
Instead of propagating individual techniques one by one, we transfer proven holistic model designs from strong source models into target model families through a shared template layer. This matters because many gains come from interactions between architectural choices, scaling decisions, and training strategies, not from isolated components applied independently.
Over the last 2 years, this approach reduced per-model engineering time by 92%, shipped 5000+ technique-model combinations across our large diverse fleet of models , while improving offline model quality by 0.63% on average at neutral serving capacity, and delivered 0.86% cumulative online lift. More importantly, it challenged a common assumption that diverse optimization goals require highly diversified model designs. In many cases, a well-designed shared template can generalize much further than expected.
We also found that once model structure is standardized, scaling decisions become more reusable. Rather than rediscovering cost-performance trade-offs separately for every model, we can learn them in template space and apply them more broadly. This led to scaling-law-based optimization workflows that make resource allocation more principled and less ad hoc.
Multi-Model Optimization
We use multi-model optimization to make template iteration rigorous. This process evaluates candidate techniques across representative models and searches for configurations that improve aggregate performance while limiting regressions.
A technique with a strong average gain but frequent regressions is difficult to ship across a large fleet. Consistency is as important as peak improvement for production-scale propagation. Multi-model optimization considers both aggregate performance and regression rate when deciding whether a technique is ready for integration.
After optimization, candidate techniques are validated on held-out models to check whether gains transfer beyond the representative set. Techniques that pass are integrated into the next template version. Over the last two years, we shipped 80 new ML techniques through this workflow.
The result is compounding. Every model that adopts a mature template inherits a history of generalized improvements rather than starting from an isolated baseline.
Why SMT Matters for Agentic ML Systems
Agentic model building often envisions a single end-to-end agent exploring a large design space with access to tools, training pipelines, and evaluation results. In practice, that approach runs into a familiar problem: The search space is too unconstrained. Without strong priors, an agent spends too much effort exploring unproductive regions, recovering from avoidable failures, or proposing changes that are difficult to explain and harder to ship.
SMT helps solve that problem because they encode known-good design patterns, which gives agents a structured starting point, a bounded search space, and a quality floor. Instead of treating model building as free-form search, we can decompose it into specialized subproblems.
At Meta, SMTs are also the foundation for our multi-agent approach to model building. Templates provide the structure, and agents provide adaptive exploration and automation. At the template level, agents help build, evaluate, and improve the templates themselves. They propose optimization ideas based on proven techniques, launch experiments across representative models, diagnose failures, and iterate over multiple rounds, which helps manage the multi-day loops that template development requires. Agents can also take on harder work such as migrating models to new hardware platforms. A technique validated this way reaches every model built from that template, at a fraction of the compute it would take to adapt each model separately. We cover this in more detail in our post, How Meta Uses AI Agents to Scale ML Techniques Across Ads Ranking Models.
Lessons Learned and the Road Ahead for SMTs
Propagating ML innovations to improve models is often the main scaling challenge in large ML ecosystems. SMTs succeed because automation gets more powerful as the underlying system becomes more structured. Template-driven development did not just make the ecosystem easier for humans to operate. It also made it easier for optimization systems, scaling workflows, and agents to reason effectively.
But standardization only works if it is opinionated enough to remove unnecessary diversity, while still preserving the limited flexibility that matters. A template system that tries to accommodate every historical edge case will eventually recreate the fragmentation it was meant to solve.
There is more work to do in improving template coverage, strengthening scaling-law-based optimization, and moving toward fully end-to-end agentic workflows — including agentic template building, model generation, online evaluation, and continuous optimization from online signals. We also need to make these workflows more reliable and more explainable.
But the central idea has held up. If you want to scale ML innovation across a large ecosystem, you need to standardize the surface on which that innovation lands. In other words, designing once and deploying at scale is not just an efficiency tactic; it is an architectural choice about how to make a large ML ecosystem learn faster.
Read the Paper
“Design Once, Deploy at Scale: Template-Driven ML Development for Large Model Ecosystems.”

posts.title: Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Meta’s Reality Labs builds products such as AI glasses. Emulators provide us with a way to scale development and testing without relying on scarce physical hardware.
Testing software for non-phone Android devices depends on how closely a virtual device reproduces the software behavior of the physical product. While a lightweight emulator like Goldfish gets you part of the way, differences from the real device can hide bugs until later in development. This lack of fidelity also erodes trust in device emulation, increasing reliance on scarce physical hardware.
Cuttlefish is the Android Open Source Project’s (AOSP’s) virtual-device framework for testing Android software against virtual hardware. It boots the same system images as real hardware and runs a realistic software stack against virtual hardware. This enables Cuttlefish to more closely track a physical device’s behavior than a lightweight emulator does.
Unfortunately, Cuttlefish is only supported on Linux, and our application and library developers work on Macs with Apple silicon. This forced us to support Goldfish and Cuttlefish side by side.
We knew if we could consolidate onto a single Cuttlefish-based platform, we could give all of our developers the benefit of the same high-fidelity virtual device. The challenge was porting the stack to make Cuttlefish run natively on macOS.
The Impact of Fragmentation
Maintaining dual emulator platforms imposed a heavy operational burden: It drained computing resources, created confusion for developers, and slowed down the emulator team. Every tool required support for two separate platforms, while infrastructure and engineering capacity were divided between them. Furthermore, developers had to choose an emulator target based on how they worked: Goldfish ran everywhere but had less fidelity while Cuttlefish needed Linux.

The AOSP mirrors this exact divide: Goldfish targets application developers, whereas Cuttlefish serves Android platform developers. So long as we maintained that division, we would suffer the effects of fragmentation.
The Stack and the macOS Gaps
Cuttlefish is the orchestration layer, while the component that actually runs the guest OS is a virtual machine monitor (VMM). On Linux, Cuttlefish normally uses crosvm but previously included support for QEMU as an alternative VMM. That integration had become inactive over time. To enable native Apple silicon support on macOS, we revived QEMU support.
Many of Cuttlefish’s virtual devices use vhost-user backends, separate processes that provide virtio devices to QEMU over a socket. The architecture is clean, but large parts of it were written with a hard Linux assumption. Three of those assumptions break on macOS. The vhost-user machinery is gated to Linux and won’t build or run. The Apple hypervisor imposes resource limits QEMU didn’t expect. Finally, the native display, build, and signing paths didn’t exist. We tackled all three.
The Cuttlefish-on-Mac stack. Cuttlefish orchestrates virtual devices backed by QEMU. The highlighted orange blocks are the Mac-specific work: adding macOS support to vhost-user, increasing memory-region tracking slots in QEMU’s HVF backend, and using the native Cocoa display and code-signing paths.
Making vhost-user Portable Beyond Linux
The most structurally important changes were in QEMU’s vhost-user path. The frontends, libvhost-user, and the contrib backends such as vhost-user-blk were all gated to Linux. We relaxed those build restrictions so the vhost-user frontends and libraries can build on macOS as well as Linux. This lets Cuttlefish’s device backends hand off to QEMU on a Mac the same way they do on Linux. Without this, the higher-fidelity device model that makes Cuttlefish worth using isn’t available outside Linux.
Living Within Hypervisor.framework
On Apple silicon, QEMU accelerates through HVF (Hypervisor.framework) instead of KVM. QEMU’s HVF backend did not track enough memory regions for larger Cuttlefish configurations. We increased its tracking-slot count so those configurations could run correctly.
A Usable Native Display
Local application development requires an interactive display allowing developers to view and engage directly with the virtual device. To enable direct interaction and bypass reliance on the WebRTC interface, we transitioned to QEMU’s native Cocoa display. The changes include:
BGRA Pixel Format Support: Enables accurate display rendering to eliminate visual artifacts on Apple silicon.
Mouse-Click-as-Touch: Translates pointer actions into touch input for interacting with touchscreen devices.
Custom Geometry Options: Adds the -g flag to graphic_console_init for display configuration.
We also enabled the unstable Rutabaga structs needed to match the Rust-side graphics ABI in gfxstream/rutabaga configurations.
Building and Signing on Apple Silicon
Finally, there was the build and packaging work: initial Darwin build support, building QEMU for arm64 on macOS, and toolchain fixes. The macOS builds also needed the JIT entitlement in addition to support for code signing and notarization. On the Cuttlefish side, we added macOS host support so the framework’s orchestration builds and runs on a Mac instead of assuming a Linux host.
The Benefits
By moving to a unified platform, we cut maintenance requirements, reduced infrastructure needs, eliminated redundant tooling, enhanced fidelity, and ensured developers run the exact same Cuttlefish virtual devices used across CI.

A single platform also made it easier to support capabilities on a shared stack, including:
Bluetooth pairing and connectivity.
Wi-Fi.
Cellular.
3D graphics.
Over-the-air (OTA) update testing to exercise over-the-air update flows against a virtual device.
Fastboot.
Snapshotting to save and restore device state in CI and development flows.
Beyond supporting Reality Labs engineers, this identical virtual device is shared with external developers building for our ecosystem. This alignment guarantees that third-party teams test against the exact same Cuttlefish-based platform we use to develop and validate the OS itself.
With AI agents playing a growing role in Android development, validation execution and runtime behavior is just as essential as code generation. Virtual devices empower both engineers and automated agents to operate concurrently within isolated environments, facilitating application execution and rapid iteration. By enabling instant state resets and repeated test runs, teams eliminate dependencies on shared physical hardware and prevent workflow interruptions. Ultimately, high-fidelity emulation ensures these continuous feedback loops are both rapid and meaningful.
Giving Back to the Community
Although we built this for development within Reality Labs, the macOS support is useful beyond our products. We’re sharing our work with the community so other developers can build on the QEMU and AOSP foundations that enabled our work.
We’re distributing the work in two parts:
qemu-wearables: a Meta-maintained fork of QEMU carrying our commits.
cuttlefish-wearables: a set of patch files, with instructions for patching Android/AOSP.
The repositories contain our QEMU changes and the Cuttlefish patch series, along with build and patch-application instructions.
We’re also exploring ways to contribute these changes upstream to QEMU and AOSP. In the meantime, developers can use our fork and patch set.
Acknowledgements
This project relies on the foundations laid by the QEMU and Cuttlefish/AOSP communities. We are particularly grateful for the vsock-user implementation created by Stefano Garzarella, which directly enabled our macOS integration.
Special thanks also go to Olya Arkhangelskaia and Tom Care at Meta for their foundational work bringing Cuttlefish to macOS, and to Jeffrey Effendy for improvements to the native Mac developer experience and subsequent productization work.
