posts.title: Engineering AI Discover
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layer
By Varun Khaitan, Peng Ren, Gary Tang, Itay Teller, Atif Faheem, Nipun Kumar, Donnie DeBoer, Eduardo Lundgren, Matteo Rinaldi, Raghav Bakshi
We recently introduced AI Discover, a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see.
Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? Our answer is a new intelligence layer, the agent harness behind AI Discover. For each request, it decides how to combine LLMs with our recommendation systems. It builds on years of work understanding what members enjoy, and on our recent work applying LLMs to recommendations and generative experiences. The layer itself plans each request, runs it across those systems, serves the result and evaluates it offline.
This post covers the challenges we designed for and the key decisions we made along the way.

Why an intelligence layer?
Every Netflix page combines recommendations with rules. We pick titles a member may enjoy, and eligibility, maturity and safety rules decide what can appear. An experience built on LLMs needs the same rules, plus code that decides when to call an LLM and how to handle its output. That code is called an agent harness, and it’s the core of our intelligence layer.
The simplest implementation hands the entire request to an LLM and lets it pick the titles, write the labels and decide what happens next. However, that leaves us relying on probabilistic output where we need governed results, because every turn in AI Discover ends on a screen in someone’s living room. At our scale, even rare failures happen many times a day. A member sees every slow call, unavailable title or off-brand line. Seven challenges shaped our design:

Fitting LLMs into a product and architecture designed without them. Traditional recommenders rank titles based on past behavior. LLMs can do more: understand what a member is asking for and plan how to respond. Our existing experience would leave most of that unused.
Keeping recommendations grounded. Every pick must be a real, available title from our changing catalog. Retrieval and rankers work in tandem with LLMs to choose titles that fit the member’s taste and intent.
Working with slow, unpredictable LLMs. LLM calls are the slowest and most expensive part of the system. Tail latencies can spike, and the output may not be what you asked for. So we use LLMs selectively, treat what they return as untrusted input and test performance and quality before anything ships.
Adapting to fast-changing models, tools and prompts. Modeling and engineering solutions keep evolving, so the product can’t depend on any single model, tool or prompt.
Building for TV. Typing on a TV is hard, so members rely on the remote, and the app should respond to every press right away on widely varying hardware. TV apps also update slowly, so changes have to ship without an app release. A typical TV request returns in moments, while multi-step generation can take several seconds.
Holding a safety and reliability bar at scale. Members always get a page, even when an LLM call fails or yields poor results. Their choices and our content standards hold on every request, and when something breaks, structured records show why.
Learning from what members say alongside what we already know. Recommendations have always learned from viewing behavior. AI Discover also lets members tell us what they want, and that has to shape what they see next.

System Architecture
When a member picks a theme, the TV app sends the request to the Page Server, which builds pages for all Netflix apps and hands the request asynchronously to the intelligence layer. At a high level, this new layer has two components: a controller and an executor.
The controller decides what to run. It gathers the context needed for each request, including real-time signals such as the time of day. It then settles on a plan, either an established one or a new one drafted by its planner, validates it and retrieves only the member details that this plan requires from Memory Hub, our per-member memory store. These details may include member taste summaries generated by MemberLLM, our in-house language model for personalized recommendations, or feedback shared by the member. We talk more about Memory Hub and member taste summaries later.
A plan is a graph of approved steps, each running a capability. A capability is a named unit of work that can have multiple versions and belongs to a family such as retrieval, ranking, generation or packaging. It declares its inputs and outputs, the context it may see and what happens if it fails.
Capability declarations make a plan verifiable. Before execution, the controller validates the graph: every step is approved, every input has a producer, nothing loops and the plan ends in exactly one page. Afterward, the controller checks the result before it’s served.
The executor runs the plan. Steps pass typed outputs to each other through the declared contracts, so each receives exactly what it asked for. Independent steps run in parallel, each with its own deadline and appropriate fallback behaviors. Some steps are optimized LLM calls with one task each, such as writing row titles or suggesting next themes, and they act only within the validated plan. Checks before the run and contracts during it give us governed execution, where every action stays within limits set in code.
Both parts write to the request records, the traces we use offline to evaluate and improve the system.
System Architecture Diagram
Key Decisions
Each challenge led to one decision. Here’s what we chose and what it bought us.
1. Design the product and architecture around LLMs
We reimagined the experience around LLMs. The easier path would have been to drop them in as rankers, keep today’s latency budgets and precompute where necessary. AI Discover is built on a back-and-forth around themes a member can steer, which gives LLMs work only they can do: generating themes, explaining rows, summarizing taste and helping choose the titles that fit the member and the moment. Members pick themes with the remote, so they never have to type. On the TV, those themes and explanations get their own native UI elements. Behind the screen, LLMs can draft plans, and asynchronous serving gives multi-step agentic orchestration the time it needs.
This opens up experiences our traditional stack couldn’t support on its own.
2. Make existing systems composable
Keeping recommendations grounded meant building on the systems that already know our catalog and members. Most capabilities wrap complex, proven Netflix systems such as search, large-scale ranking and catalog metadata access. Some of them may run their own agents in the future.
Reshaping them took careful work, because agentic orchestration challenges many long-standing assumptions of distributed systems. A capability now has to work in combinations no one designed, for a caller that chooses to call it at runtime. Each one needs a clear purpose and a semantic interface, and shaping it means deciding how much to combine into a single step and how much to leave to the planner. Too fine, and the planner has more ways to go wrong; too coarse, and it loses room to compose richer plans.
In return, the planner gets building blocks it can mix in new ways, and connecting services takes far less manual wiring. Because plans can only use these blocks, even one drafted on the fly stays grounded in our catalog and member taste.
3. Plan first, then execute
To contain LLM latency and errors, we plan every request before anything runs. The familiar way to let an agent use tools is a loop: reason, call a tool, read the result, reason again. It’s flexible, but you can’t tell up front how many steps it will take or whether it has gone down a wrong path. In agent terms, ours is a plan-and-execute agent: an LLM can propose the path, but code decides whether it runs.
Plans come from two places: established plans we’ve already tested, and plans an LLM drafts on the fly. A router we control decides which one is served. Either way, the plan passes the same checks before it runs. If the planner is slow or its plan fails a check, we fall back to a tested plan.
This allows for adaptive planning. The planner can find new ways to serve a request, and we can balance cost, latency and quality for each task, from a lean single-call plan to a richer multi-step one.

4. Stay model and capability agnostic
The best model or capability for a task today may be second-best, or overkill, in a few months, so we built the system to switch between them. We assign each task to the model or capability version that fits it. Today that’s a per-task setting we can override live. Only some steps in a request use an LLM.
That only works if switching is easy. All the LLMs we use sit behind one common interface. Before we switch, each candidate is scored on the same tasks by automated checks and LLM judges, so every swap is a measured change.
Much of the system’s behavior lives in server-side prompts and configuration, so we can swap models, tools and capabilities without new code or a TV app release.
Upgrades get cheap and experiments get easy. Moving to a better model, ranker or retrieval system is a plan or setting change, not a migration, so each component can keep improving without a large investment.
5. Make page generation asynchronous
Inference keeps getting faster, but member expectations rise just as quickly: richer responses, more context and more of the page shaped by LLMs. The line between what feels instant and what’s worth waiting for will keep shifting, so we built the asynchronous path as a first-class way of serving.
Most of a TV app is synchronous: press a button, get a page. Generative work breaks that pattern. Holding one request open for many seconds across services would tie up too many threads. So requests that involve generation are asynchronous. The press returns right away with an acknowledgement, and the TV switches to a thinking state that explains what’s being prepared. Meanwhile, the executor runs the plan in the background. When the result is ready, the server notifies the TV, which then fetches it.
Slow generation no longer slows anything else. The serving path stays healthy however long a turn takes, and every press still gets immediate feedback on screen.
Async Sequence Diagram
6. Enforce safety in code
Some rules must hold no matter what an LLM writes: content and maturity standards, what each step can access, and what a member has asked us not to show them. Putting those rules in a prompt makes them probabilistic, so we enforce them in code. Generated text is cleaned up before it reaches the screen. The planner sees a stripped-down request, and member details are limited to what the validated plan needs.
For example, the planner decides which inputs each step needs, such as the profile’s maturity rating for retrieval. Instead of writing parameter values directly, it uses placeholders. After the plan passes validation, the controller fills them with values from the request, matched by declared type. This also protects against prompt injection.
Each request also leaves a structured record: the plan, each step and its outcome, and which rules applied. When a page misses, we can tell whether the plan, the data, a rule or the model was at fault. The same records feed our offline evaluation and replay.
Together, these rules and records let an experiment ship at the same safety and privacy bar as the rest of the product.
7. Remember what members tell us
A taste summary is a short profile of what a member enjoys, such as favorite genres, tone and recurring themes. MemberLLM generates it ahead of time from the member’s viewing history, which keeps that LLM work off the request path. It helps us further personalize their page, and steps that write themes and explanations receive it as context, so their wording reflects the member. We’ll cover MemberLLM in more detail in an upcoming post.
In AI Discover, members can also tune their recommendations and tell us directly what they want. Those choices apply right away and carry across visits, and they give us a new signal alongside what we already know about their taste. This is a first step toward remembering more about each member, from their preferences to the habits that show up over time and the corners of the catalog they like to explore. We keep it all in Memory Hub, our persistent, low-latency memory store, next to their taste summaries, and we can add new kinds of memory as we need them. We apply these memories to later requests where they’re relevant, together with real-time context.
The member holds the remote
In this version, members interact by selecting themes and using tuning options such as “don’t recommend.” There’s no free-text input or open-ended chat. That keeps the LLM’s job narrow by design.

The usual protections still apply. Profile settings and our safety and privacy policies hold here as everywhere else.
Generated text was tested before launch. We ran safety evaluations on theme labels, row titles and explanations to make sure they meet our standards.

What’s next
It would have been faster to let an LLM do everything and stop there. The intelligence layer gave us an AI-native product, grounded building blocks, adaptive planning, quicker experimentation, asynchronous generation, governed execution and agent memory for tunable personalization. While AI Discover is its first experience, we designed it with more in mind.
We’ve organized our efforts to answer two questions:

How much do members want to shape their recommendations? Whether they’d rather steer or lean back, and how much, which kinds of themes help, and how we should blend what members tell us with our existing personalization systems.
What tradeoffs does this technology bring? How cost and latency hold up in production as we ramp traffic, how long members will wait for generated results, and whether errors came from the model, the harness or our existing systems. Multi-turn sessions also need different evaluation and observability than single requests.

Longer term, our goal is a system that improves itself, starting from the record each request leaves behind. Today we replay past requests against a new prompt, model or rule to see what changes, and we judge each change with automated checks, LLM judges and human evaluations. Eventually, we want the system to propose improvements, test them safely and keep only what proves better, within our privacy and data-use policies. As LLMs improve, more of the work may move into them, and the intelligence layer lets us move that line deliberately.
This is part of a bigger shift. Recommendation systems have long learned quietly from what members watch and answered with ranked rows. LLMs let them listen and respond, and members may increasingly expect that. We’ll keep exploring what that means for discovery on Netflix.
Acknowledgements
We would like to thank Adi Suresh, Akash Katipally, Allan Johns, Becks Wood, Bhargav Mangipudi, Carrie Santiago, Chris Martin, Claire Campbell, Corey Waldin, Dana Sittler, Daneo Zhang, David Leen, Devon Bryant, Dharamendra Kumar, Dharini Chandrasekaran, Ebony Turner, Federico Roa, Gianfranco Cuoco, Guru Tahasildar, Haley Clanton, Haresh Chudgar, Ivan Provalov, James Schultz, JingXu Yang, Josie Shaw, Kamelia Aryafar, Kate Cummings, Kathleen Garrity, Kelley Robinson, Kevin Du, Kevin O’Connor, Kyla Moore, Kyle Lind, Laura Matsuura, Leah Cusella, Lingyi Liu, Lingyong Wang, Mallory Walkup, Matthew Pereira, Michael Galassi, Minsu Jang, Moumita Bhattacharya, Paran Jain, Paul Lee, Qusai Al-Rabadi, Scarlet Chen, Sergi Perez, Sriram Rao, Stephen Shaw, Sura Elamurugu, Varad Pathak, Yesu Feng, Zainab Mahar Mir, and Zhongli Cheng for their contributions to this work.

posts.title: Under the Hood of Native WSL Mode in RubyMine: IJent and EelApi
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
RubyMine’s WSL support has evolved over many years, resulting in several ways of working with projects in WSL. Starting with the 2026.3 release, there is one recommended way to work with a project stored in WSL – Native WSL mode: open or clone the project directly from the Welcome screen and use native WSL interpreters to run Ruby.
The IDE remains a Windows application, while a lightweight agent inside WSL handles files and processes.
Native mode and the IJent agent
To give your IDE seamless access to the Linux filesystem, processes, and other environment resources, we built IJent, a lightweight agent made just for this job. Because IJent is designed specifically for IDE workflows, we can shape its behavior, protocol, and capabilities around what developers actually need, so working with Linux feels as smooth and responsive as working locally.
Together, the IDE and IJent form a client-server pair. This may resemble the remote development model, but the server component is much thinner and more versatile.
This particular technology stack helps us address several important challenges:
Rust implementation: Rust keeps the executable slim. By not relying on Java or Kotlin for the agent, we eliminate additional runtime dependencies inside containers or WSL environments.




Transport layer: stdio provides a portable, firewall-friendly transport across all environments. Hyper-V sockets on WSL offer a faster path, which is especially beneficial for large or numerous filesystem transfers.




Correct filesystem semantics: IJent executes filesystem operations on behalf of the IDE inside the target environment. As a result, path resolution, including symbolic links, follows correct Linux semantics. Third-party plugins also benefit from this model, since their file operations are routed through IJent.
EelApi: One interface for any environment
To make full use of IJent in RubyMine, changes on the IDE side are also required. That’s where EelApi comes in.
EelApi is an API designed to abstract away the distinction between local and remote environments for everyone writing IDE-related code, including plugin authors and platform contributors.
With EelApi, developers don’t need to handle environment-specific differences themselves. The same IDE code can work across local environments, WSL, Docker, and Dev Containers without needing to know where it’s running.
In general, IJent implements the EelApi interface, providing the functionality that EelApi exposes to the IDE and plugins.
If you’re interested in a more detailed explanation of EelApi, together with a practical introduction, readThe Dev Containers Story: Introducing EelApi for Plugin Authors.
Performance tests
We conducted performance tests to compare working with remote interpreters (based on the 9P filesystem protocol) and Native mode. The results show a clear performance improvement with the new approach:




The test results represent the median of five measured runs performed on Windows 11 using WSL 2 and Ubuntu 24.04.
While Native mode is now our recommended way to work with WSL projects, the other two methods (remote development and remote interpreters) remain supported.
However, from now on we’ll be focusing our development efforts on Native WSL mode. This means other ways to work with WSL projects will no longer receive major feature updates or usability improvements, and only critical regressions will be addressed.
Thank you for reading and for all the feedback that helped us reach this point. Let us know how Native mode performs with your projects.
Follow RubyMine on X for more updates and insights.
The RubyMine team

posts.title: LinkedIn Connected Apps 1.2: Clearer Level System, Visible Progress, and Direct Answers About Privacy
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
What if your LinkedIn profile reflected how you actually build software instead of just being a list of your skills? That’s what the LinkedIn Connected Apps plugin does: It tracks how you use your JetBrains IDE, awards you a level ranking, and provides a descriptive statement associated with your level that you can choose to share.
Since the first version came out, you’ve told us what works and what doesn’t. The level system wasn’t entirely clear and you wanted a plain explanation of what happens to your data.
Version 1.2 is built around that feedback. It introduces four levels based on real work that gets done in the IDE, a widget that shows your progress and what’s next, and a clear account of what stays on your machine.
Get the plugin
                                                    
What’s new in 1.2
Levels based on how you use your IDE
The leveling path now has four levels instead of five, and each one reflects what developers do in their IDE on a day-to-day basis. There are two distinct branches, Coding and AI, with the AI branch starting at Level 3. Because everyone starts at Level 1, you must progress through the first two levels on the Coding branch before starting on the AI branch. The branches are independent, so your Coding level and AI level can be different.
Imagine this progression, for example. Shortly after getting started with your IDE, you use code completion and reach Level 1. You continue using core functionality more broadly, searching for code throughout the project, so the next day you reach Level 2. You then start refactoring and using Git, so you reach Level 3 in Coding. Later you start working on tasks via AI chat, bringing you to Level 3 in AI. Eventually you start running AI agents and reviewing their changes, so you reach Level 4 in AI, even while you’re still at Level 3 on the Coding side. Your profile shows the level you’ve reached on each branch.

LevelCodingAI

1Use a core IDE capability, for example, search, code completion, or code navigation.–
2Search for code across the project, type with code completion, or navigate to declarations or usages.–
3Refactor by renaming or moving elements, run commands in the terminal, run your application or configurations, or use Git through the UI (commit, fetch, or update).Work on coding tasks with AI to generate and explain code, run AI agents (such as Junie, Claude, or Codex) in the integrated terminal, or complete tasks using JetBrains Air.

4Debug with the integrated debugger (Step Over, Step Into, Evaluate Expression), work with editor shortcuts, apply advanced refactorings (Extract and Introduce), and use the Git Log and Diff view.Use AI agents to generate, refactor, and explain code. Orchestrate agents or run tasks through the integrated terminal or JetBrains Air, then review their changes in the Diff view.





For more information about how levels are calculated in a particular IDE, check out the help center for IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, PhpStorm, Rider, GoLand, CLion, RustRover, or RubyMine.
Always know what’s next
A widget shows your current level and the statement that goes with it, and explains what you’ll need to do to reach the next one. Each requirement has a progress counter and is marked with a check once completed, allowing you to track your progress at a glance and always have a clear view of what remains to be done.








For the bigger picture, switch to the tree view. It shows every level at once, including where the Coding and AI branches split at Level 3. It also marks which levels you’ve completed, which one you’re on, and which ones are still ahead. Click on any level to see exactly what it requires.




Privacy and your data
In response to your questions, here are some important details about how the plugin uses your data:
When you do something that counts toward a level, the plugin records it locally. This usage data stays on your computer and is not shared with LinkedIn. The plugin doesn’t change your IDE data sharing settings.
After you connect your LinkedIn account and reach a new level, the IDE sends only the corresponding statement.
You connect through LinkedIn’s own OAuth 2.0 page in your browser. The plugin never sees or stores your LinkedIn password. It receives only an access token and a refresh token, which it keeps in the IDE’s secure credential store.
That token lets the plugin do one thing: add and update your JetBrains IDE statement in the Connected Apps section of your profile. The plugin doesn’t read any other part of your profile.
You can end the connection at any time. Simply click Disconnect from LinkedIn in the plugin, and revoke the app’s access from your LinkedIn settings under Data privacy | Permitted services.
If you already have a statement on your profile
The statements you’ve already achieved stay as they are. Once you earn a new statement, the statement on your LinkedIn profile will also be updated.
How your existing progress carries over
If you were already using the first version of the plugin, your existing progress should generally carry over to the new four-level scheme. Here’s how the levels have changed:
Level 1 and Level 2 are unchanged.
The old Level 3 is now split into Level 3 Coding and Level 3 AI.
The old Level 4 is now split into Level 4 Coding and Level 4 AI.
The old Level 5 has been removed, and the activities associated with it have been merged into Level 4 of Coding and AI.
Your previously achieved levels will be mapped to the corresponding levels in the new scheme based on your recorded activity. In some cases, particularly when switching devices or IDEs, certain progress may not carry over completely.
How to get started
In your IDE, go to Settings | Plugins.
On the Marketplace tab, search for “LinkedIn Connected Apps” and click Install, or Update if you already have it.
Click the Your IDE Proficiency widget in the lower right corner to see your level and next steps.
When you’re ready to share your statement, click Connect to LinkedIn and follow the instructions in your browser.





The plugin is free and supports IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, PhpStorm, Rider, GoLand, CLion, RustRover, and RubyMine, version 2025.3 or later. DataGrip isn’t supported. For the full list of level requirements, see the documentation.
Open the widget, see where you are, and let us know what you think in the comments.
FAQ
Is this a certification?
This plugin reflects how you use your IDE and doesn’t measure your skills as a developer. It is not a certification.
Do I have to share my level on LinkedIn?
Connecting to LinkedIn is totally optional. Until you connect, your level is stored only on your machine.
What data is shared with LinkedIn and JetBrains?
Your feature usage is tracked locally and isn’t shared with LinkedIn. After you connect, only your statement ID is sent when you reach a new level. The plugin doesn’t change your existing IDE data sharing settings, so no new data will be shared with JetBrains.
Do I need to keep the plugin installed after connecting?
Yes, if you want your progress to keep updating on LinkedIn. You can also share your level once and remove the plugin.
Can I connect multiple IDEs?
Yes. Each connected IDE gets its own statement on your profile.
Is the plugin free?
Yes, the plugin is free and works in IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, PhpStorm, Rider, GoLand, CLion, RustRover, and RubyMine, version 2025.3 or later. DataGrip isn’t supported. For the full list of level requirements, see the documentation.

posts.title: Sky’s the Limit: The Cloud9 × JetBrains Global Hackathon Is Back
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Sky’s the Limit is back! Join Cloud9 and JetBrains for the next edition of our global hackathon.
Last year, around 2,300 participants registered, and we received 180 project submissions, ranging from coaching tools and scouting assistants to games for fans. You can read about the results and winning projects here. This year, we’d love to see even more of you participate.
Gaming is a big part of developers’ lives. In our State of Developer Ecosystem Report 2026, we saw that it remains their most popular hobby. This hackathon is an opportunity to bring gaming and programming together.




From November 17, 2026, to January 12, 2027, you can build tools for Cloud9’s coaches or a minigame for fans to play at events. There are three main categories, a bonus award, and USD 25,000 in cash prizes up for grabs. The winners of the three main categories will also receive GDC tickets, round-trip flights, and hotel accommodation.
Register for the hackathon






Two months of free access to JetBrains tools and AI Ultimate for every participant
Everyone taking part in the hackathon will receive promo codes for two months of free access to the JetBrains All Products Pack and JetBrains AI Ultimate.
You’ll have access to JetBrains IDEs and the AI credits included with AI Ultimate, so you can experiment with coding agents via JetBrains Air in your IDE while building your project.
Once you receive your participant codes, redeem your two months of free access to JetBrains All Products Pack and JetBrains AI Ultimate. Use the same email address for both, then follow the activation links sent to your inbox to add the subscriptions to your JetBrains Account.
Try JetBrains Air in your IDE
This year, we especially encourage you to try JetBrains Air in IDEs, our new layer for agentic development inside your JetBrains IDE.
Air lets you work with multiple coding agents, including Codex, Claude Agent, Gemini, Cursor, Junie, and more through ACP, with support for models from different providers. You can run agents in parallel, track their progress, and guide their work as your project develops.
The IDE’s understanding of your code provides supported agents with useful context and tools to find their way around your project. You also have the IDE’s tools for navigation, inspections, diff views, and testing to review changes and verify the results.
We encourage you to try Junie Lite, the free model tier for Junie, our coding agent. Junie Lite will remain free until at least December 31, 2026. It doesn’t use your AI credits, so you can experiment with everyday coding tasks, such as making small edits or writing tests, without it costing you a thing. You can share your experience with any of our tools, including JetBrains IDEs, Air in IDEs, or Junie Lite, in the bonus category described below.
We’ll host office hours and a live JetBrains Air demo during the hackathon. We’ll show you how to get set up, work with agents, and review their output – and there’ll be an interactive session afterward, where you can ask any questions you might have.
Office hours and Air demo: Wednesday, December 9, 2026, at 10:00 am PT / 7:00 pm CET.
To get started, visit the Air in IDEs product page, configure your agent access, and follow our step-by-step guide to starting your first agent session.
What you can build
Choose one of the three categories below. Your entry can be a new application or a significant update to an existing one, and it must use at least one eligible JetBrains tool.
Official VALORANT and League of Legends esports data from GRID will be available to participants. However, using it is optional in all categories.
VALORANT tactical scouting, utility placement, and Operator profiling
Build a scouting tool for professional VALORANT and Game Changers coaching staff. You could help coaches analyze ability usage and utility placement, or study opponents’ Operator positions, opening engagements, and weapon-buy patterns.
Follow one of the suggested blueprints or develop your own scouting tool to help coaches prepare for matches.
League of Legends macro scouting and draft management
Build a tool that makes match preparation easier for League of Legends coaches. You could automate macro scouting, help analyze opponents’ tendencies, or create a draft organizer that tracks champion pools, picks, bans, and Fearless Draft restrictions across a series.
The goal is to help coaching staff spend less time organizing information and more time using it.
Event minigame
Create a minigame that fans can play at a Cloud9 or JetBrains booth or event. Think simple controls, quick rounds, and a score or result that makes people want to play again.
Reaction challenges, aim trainers, and short strategy games are a few possible directions. Use original names, artwork, and assets, and check the full category requirements on Devpost.
Bonus award: Best AI-Powered Workflow Story
Alongside your main entry, you can submit a short case study, blog post, social media post, or video about how you used JetBrains IDEs, Air, or Junie to build your project.
Tell us what you tried, where the tools helped, and what you learned. For example, you could show how you split work between agents, provided context, or reviewed and improved their changes.
This is an optional bonus entry tied to your project in one of the three main categories.
Judges
Judges from Cloud9 and JetBrains will review the submissions. They’ll consider how you used JetBrains tools, the design, the problem your project solves, the originality of the idea, and how clearly you demonstrate it working.
Prizes
The hackathon has a USD 25,000 cash prize pool:

AwardCash prizeGDC prize

Winner in each of the three main categoriesUSD 6,000GDC tickets, round-trip economy flights, and hotel accommodation
Runner-up in each of the three main categoriesUSD 2,000–
Best AI-Powered Workflow StoryUSD 1,000–





Each prize also includes a USD 100 Cloud9 Store gift card and a one-year individual subscription to the JetBrains All Products Pack.
Last year’s main category winners joined us at GDC in San Francisco, where some presented their projects at JetBrains GameDev Night. The winning minigame was also playable at our booth.
See the hackathon page for eligibility, travel details, and the full prize terms.
Important dates

posts.title: Kotlin Toolchain 0.14: Agentic Development and iOS Publishing
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
The Kotlin Toolchain helps you build and ship multiplatform apps faster, with less setup and configuration. Its CLI provides a unified workflow for building, running, testing, and publishing apps for Android, iOS, desktop, and web, whether you’re developing with AI agents or writing code yourself.
Kotlin Toolchain 0.14 makes it easier to publish iOS apps to TestFlight and brings improvements to agentic development workflows, along with several other enhancements.
Install Kotlin Toolchain
         
Or try this prompt in your favorite agent: 
Create a new Kotlin Multiplatform app for Android, iOS, desktop, and web with the Kotlin Toolchain CLI (https://kotlin-toolchain.org/latest).
Copy
To access the latest Kotlin Toolchain features from your IDE, use IntelliJ IDEA 2026.2.4 (or newer) or Android Studio Rabbit 1 | 2026.2.1 (or newer). Make sure the latest version of the Kotlin Toolchain plugin is installed.
iOS application publishing
You can now publish iOS apps using the kotlin publish testflight command.
This launches an easy publishing flow that guides you through most of the setup and steps required to publish a new application to TestFlight for the first time. After the first publication, you can publish updates automatically using the same command.
The command will ask for an App Store Connect access token (Apple Developer Program membership is required, as usual), which is a standard way to authorize automations to publish applications in App Store Connect. We never save the private key itself or ask for Apple ID credentials.




Note that you can also still access an Xcode project and use that to set up publishing with manual signing and other advanced options, if necessary.
For more information see the documentation.
Agentic workflows support
The Kotlin CLI wizard now helps configure agents by generating relevant files in your project, such as MCP server configuration and an AGENTS.md file. These files provide general recommendations for agents to help them act more accurately and reduce the development feedback loop.
We also added Kotlin Toolchain skills as part of the Kotlin agent skills collection.
To install the skills, run in your terminal:
npx skills add kotlin/kotlin-agent-skills
Our AI evals show that using these skills helps to reduce the token consumption of working with Kotlin Toolchain-based projects.




Error and warning visibility in templates in the IDE
Now, when a module has errors or warnings originating from the template application, the IDE displays the problem both at its source and the template application.




If a template issue only arises upon application (e.g., via module dependency conflicts), the template message includes a hint specifying when it occurs.




Java 8+ API desugaring for Android
Android’s core library desugaring is now supported natively by the Kotlin Toolchain: a single desugaring: enabled line in module.yaml turns it on, with the desugaring library itself overridable via the library option. See the settings reference for more details.
Customizable external tool download URLs
The Kotlin Toolchain downloads the external tools it needs under the hood, and every location it downloads from is now documented and overridable with an environment variable. This makes it possible to route all downloads through internal mirrors, whether to comply with corporate network policies or to avoid Maven Central’s rate limits.
Dependency resolution optimization
The first import of a project – the one where every dependency has to be resolved and downloaded from the network – just got significantly faster. According to our benchmarks, importing the Kotlin Toolchain project itself without caches is now more than 3x faster. The updated resolver makes fewer unnecessary requests to repositories, downloads more dependencies in parallel, and still ensures that all downloaded files are valid.
Install Kotlin Toolchain 0.14.0
Ready to start building with the Kotlin Toolchain?
Check out our Getting started guide to dive into code examples, tutorials, or explore the comprehensive user guide to learn more.
Install Kotlin Toolchain
         
Or try this prompt in your favorite agent: 
Create a new Kotlin Multiplatform app for Android, iOS, desktop, and web with the Kotlin Toolchain CLI (https://kotlin-toolchain.org/latest).
Copy
Share your feedback
Have feedback or ideas? Join the conversation in the #kotlin-toolchain Slack channel (get invite: kotl.in/slack) or share your suggestions and ideas in JetBrains YouTrack. Your input and use cases help shape the future of the Kotlin Toolchain!

posts.title: Backporting the Improvements of PhpStorm Light to PhpStorm
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
TL;DR: PhpStorm Light validated the ideas that will define where PhpStorm goes next. It won’t continue as a standalone product – instead, we’re folding its key improvements into the main PhpStorm.
You may have never heard of PhpStorm Light, or you may be using it and wondering if this Early Access build is ever going to make its way into a major release.
In this post, we explain what PhpStorm Light is, what we’ve learned from this experiment, and what’s happening next.




What is PhpStorm Light?
PhpStorm Light has been available since June under the Early Access Program (EAP) as an experimental, trimmed-down build of PhpStorm. Its goal was to test quickly and boldly which optimizations could improve startup time, reduce memory consumption, and eliminate whatever slows PHP developers down – without disrupting the workflows they rely on. 
Like every JetBrains IDE, PhpStorm is built on the IntelliJ Platform and benefits from many of the improvements introduced there. For example, version 2026.3 added an agent-first development workspace, a projectless Welcome screen, and separate worktrees for PR/MR reviews.
PhpStorm Light, on the other hand, focuses on tools, project structures, and workflows that are specific to PHP development. We experimented with:
Faster startup: Smarter project scanning and indexing order, less unnecessary work during startup, and clearer indexing progress.
Smoother editing: A lighter inspection profile by default, a smart mode toggler, and other optimizations.
Lighter footprint: Not loading tools (e.g. for databases) until you actually need them, and making rarely used features and plugins opt-in.
Why a separate build?
We wanted to explore what would happen if we rethought some of PhpStorm’s long-standing defaults. But it’s hard to test this in a regular release that development teams rely on every day. Changing what loads at startup, which inspections run by default, and which plugins come bundled affects everyone at once.
A separate build gave us the freedom to experiment with these changes and gather feedback from PHP developers who had opted in and understood what they were testing. 
That is also why it’s distributed separately: PhpStorm Light is an experiment, not a product.
What we’ve learned
Much of the overhead is work you haven’t asked for yet. PhpStorm does a lot in the background as soon as a project opens: checking for updates, scanning for places to make suggestions, and preparing information you may never look at. In PhpStorm Light, this work is deferred until you actually need it. This means less work during startup and while you’re typing.
Faster doesn’t have to mean fewer features. PhpStorm Light changes what’s enabled by default, not what is available. Features and plugins that aren’t enabled out of the box are still there, and you can enable them whenever you need them.
Not every change is right for everyone. Some of the new defaults will not suit every developer or workflow. We’re still evaluating them, and we are open to your feedback.
So, here’s the plan: We’re bringing some of PhpStorm Light’s improvements right into PhpStorm, making sure that every change to a long-standing default comes with a simple way to restore the previous behavior.
What’s next?
If you’re using the standard PhpStorm build, several PhpStorm Light improvements will arrive through regular updates. We’ll explain each change when it ships. There is no need to install a separate build.
If you’re using PhpStorm Light, nothing changes for now. However, PhpStorm Light builds will eventually be discontinued once the changes are merged into the mainstream PhpStorm build. 
Thank you to everyone who tried this experimental build and took the time to tell us what worked and what didn’t. 
Is there anything else we should take into account? Let us know in the comments to this blog post or provide your feedback on YouTrack. Your input is helping shape the future of PhpStorm.

posts.title: AI-Generated Code Security Risks: What Qodana Found in a Java App
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Adding search functionality, converting a document, or connecting a service sound like small changes. An AI coding agent may take it on in one pass, changing application logic, dependencies, configuration, and tests along the way. The result may pass functional tests and still contain security vulnerabilities.
Static analysis can surface some AI-generated code security risks, while reviewers and targeted tests determine which findings matter in practice. Where can external input travel? What happens if a configuration value is missing? Do the new dependencies introduce risks the functional tests never exercise? The same questions matter in any codebase, including code written with AI. 
A study of AI-generated Python and JavaScript snippets in public GitHub projects found weaknesses across 43 Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) categories. OWASP recommends reviewing any fully agent-produced changes, including dependencies and tests. Passing tests are useful evidence, but they don’t answer every security question. 
Static analysis gives reviewers a place to start. It can point to data flows, unsafe code patterns, vulnerable dependencies, and hardcoded values, but each finding still needs context. A reviewer must check whether the path is reachable, what runs in production, and which fix fits the application. 
Table of Contents

Why AI-generated code still needs a security review
Scanning the Corporate Payments Portal with Qodana
What Qodana found in the application
A vulnerable dependency and an XML-processing call
A hardcoded fallback remains in configuration
A license finding raises a different question

How to use the findings in a security review
FAQ


Why AI-generated code still needs a security review
An agent may implement the requested behavior while missing constraints that live outside the feature description. Passing functional tests may still leave questions about how data crosses trust boundaries or how deployment settings affect security. OWASP’s secure code review guidance calls for understanding business requirements, tracing data flows, and checking configuration and deployment. These checks often span modules.
Qodana points to relevant paths and patterns, then reviewers supply the application context needed to judge them.
Scanning the Corporate Payments Portal with Qodana
We examined the Corporate Payments Portal, a Java app from the RealVuln Benchmark, alongside its public Qodana report. The benchmark deliberately seeds vulnerabilities in AI-generated code, giving us concrete findings to investigate. We’ll follow several of them from the code to the questions a reviewer would ask. This single case does not tell us how often AI introduces vulnerabilities.
The Corporate Payments Portal uses Java 21 and Spring Boot and includes a web portal, a payment API, a mock core banking service, and a batch worker. We use a pinned source revision so the excerpts match the report. That matters because a risky flow may begin with a controller and end with a service, while a dependency or configuration value can create a separate concern even when a Java method looks ordinary.
We ran a focused Qodana scan for data flows, vulnerable dependencies, hardcoded passwords, and dependency licenses. The password inspection was configured more broadly than its defaults for this example. Qodana’s findings provide starting points – a trace can show where data may travel, and a dependency alert can identify a version with known advisories. Neither, by itself, settles whether a specific attack is reachable in this deployment.
What Qodana found in the application
The public Qodana report lists 65 findings across 21 files. That is a triage queue, not a count of exploitable vulnerabilities. Alerts repeat across modules, and some point to synthetic values in tests and documentation. The examples below show how a finding can lead to a concrete question about code, configuration, or dependencies.
A vulnerable dependency and an XML-processing call
The Corporate Payments Portal’s web module parses XML drafts using XStream. Its build file, portal/build.gradle, declares version 1.4.7:
implementation 'com.thoughtworks.xstream:xstream:1.4.7'




Qodana’s dependency check flags this version and lists known advisories. A separate taint finding points to the call that turns the XML string into Java objects:
new com.thoughtworks.xstream.XStream().fromXML(draft)




These two signals answer different questions. The dependency alert says the application includes a version with known issues. The fromXML(draft) call takes its XML from the cpDeskDraft browser cookie. The controller checks only whether the cookie is empty. Because a client can change its cookie, this is considered untrusted input. XStream 1.4.7 does not use a type allowlist by default, so deserialization can instantiate unintended types. The exact impact depends on the payload and runtime environment.
The taint finding is labeled path traversal in this report, and the vulnerable API usage inspection did not produce a separate result. It would be misleading to tie a specific CVE to this call from these findings alone. Review whether XML deserialization is needed at all. If it is, update the dependency, allow only expected types, and test that unexpected XML is rejected.
A hardcoded fallback remains in configuration
In the Corporate Payments Portal’s payment API, the legacy report bridge reads an intake key from a Spring configuration property. The colon inside the Spring placeholder defines a fallback value:
legacy-report-bridge:
  intake-key: ${LEGACY_REPORT_BRIDGE_KEY:legacy-bridge-dev-key-9c1e}








Spring reads the value after the colon when LEGACY_REPORT_BRIDGE_KEY is absent. The same fallback also appears in LegacyReportBridge‘s Java constructor. That component sends the resulting key to an internal reporting service as a bridge-key query parameter. In this benchmark, the value is synthetic, but a deployment that omits the environment variable could silently use a credential stored in source control.
Qodana’s Hardcoded passwords inspection flagged this example after we enabled detection based on suspicious variable names. Its default configuration would not flag this exact pattern. For production, remove the fallback in both the application.yml and LegacyReportBridge‘s @Value annotation. Require the key from an external secret source and fail startup if it is missing. Keep any development default confined to a development profile, and confirm whether the bridge is enabled in deployed environments.
For another example of Qodana detecting a hardcoded password, watch Helen’s video walkthrough:






A license finding raises a different question
One finding concerns dependency policy rather than an exploitable bug. In the Corporate Payments Portal, Qodana’s license audit flags hibernate-core 6.5.3.Final, brought in transitively, because its LGPL-2.1-or-later license is on the report’s prohibited list for a project marked PROPRIETARY-LICENSE. Transitive means another dependency brings the component into the build; it may not appear in the developer’s direct dependency list.
The risk is making a distribution decision without reviewing the dependency’s obligations. This is a policy signal, not a legal conclusion or evidence that hibernate-core is insecure. A reviewer should confirm the project’s actual policy and distribution model, review the applicable terms, and then document an accepted exception or choose another dependency path. Repeated alerts across modules do not necessarily represent different libraries.
How to use the findings in a security review
An alert becomes useful when it changes a review decision. The examples give us different kinds of evidence, and each leaves a different question open. The table summarizes selected signals:

PatternWhat Qodana showsReview question
Vulnerable dependencyAdvisories and an XML callWhat objects could XStream create from this cookie?
Credential fallbackConstant key in configurationCould the fallback run in production?
License policyTransitive license policy alertDoes the project policy allow it?





A developer using JetBrains Air can open an agent’s diffs in context and leave comments on specific lines for the agent to act on. Qodana adds a different view, scanning the codebase and reporting issues found by its inspections. The developer can weigh both when deciding what to fix. The findings discussed in this article were derived solely from Qodana.




From there, the team checks whether input reaches each operation, whether an affected component is actually used, and which configuration applies in deployment. It fixes the relevant code or policy, tests the change, and records why any remaining alerts are accepted or dismissed. Supported checks can also run in CI, so later changes receive the same review signals.
Static analysis makes these questions visible and repeatable. It helps the team spend review time on specific paths and components, while developers supply the application context and decide whether a change is ready to ship.
You can explore the evidence in our public report. If you would like to run the experiment yourself, leave a comment, and we’ll get in touch to help with the setup.
Explore Qodana’s Report
FAQ
Is AI-generated code more vulnerable than human-written code?
There is no universal answer. Results depend on the tool, task, application context, and review process. This deliberately vulnerable benchmark cannot establish a comparative rate.
Can static analysis detect every security issue in AI-generated code?
No. It can identify supported patterns and trace some data flows, but it can miss application-specific authorization rules and runtime behavior. Combine it with human review and targeted testing.
Can Qodana automatically secure AI-generated code?
Qodana can automate supported inspections and surface findings for triage. It cannot determine whether every flagged path is exploitable or whether the application’s security requirements are complete.
Book a demo
Get more practical insights on code quality and security. Subscribe to the Qodana blog for new posts.

posts.title: Run AI Agents in TeamCity
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
AI coding agents don’t have to run only on a developer’s machine. You can also make them part of your CI/CD workflows to review code, investigate failed builds, update documentation, or handle other repository tasks.
The new experimental AI Agents plugin for TeamCity lets you run Codex and Claude Code directly in TeamCity builds and connect them to the LLM provider of your choice.
The plugin installs the coding agent on the TeamCity build agent, provides credentials safely for the duration of the build, and collects usage statistics and agent trajectories. 
When a build starts, the plugin checks whether the selected client is available and installs it if necessary. You can then call codex or claude from a regular TeamCity Command Line build step. 
Install the plugin
What does the AI Agents plugin do?
The plugin handles much of the setup needed to run coding agents reliably in CI.
Connect to your preferred LLM provider
The plugin stores your provider credentials as a TeamCity connection. It currently supports:
JetBrains Air
OpenAI
Anthropic
LiteLLM
OpenRouter
This is not limited to models provided directly by these services. Gateways such as OpenRouter and LiteLLM give you access to a much wider range of models, so you can choose models and providers that make sense for your team.
Run Codex and Claude Code without preinstalling them
You don’t have to install Codex or Claude Code manually on every TeamCity build agent. When a build starts, the plugin checks whether the selected client is available and installs it if necessary. You can then call codex or claude from a regular TeamCity Command Line build step.
Keep provider credentials out of your build agents
TeamCity build agents are often reused across builds, so leaving provider credentials on an agent can be a security risk. The plugin provides the necessary credentials to the TeamCity agent only for the duration of the build and removes them afterward. 
Your provider credentials are managed through the TeamCity connection rather than permanently stored on individual build agents.
Track token usage
The plugin collects usage statistics from agent runs and publishes them as TeamCity statistical values, including prompt, completion, cached, and total token counts.
Because these are regular TeamCity statistics, you can use them to track AI usage over time and create charts. This can also help you spot unexpected changes in token consumption and investigate possible cost anomalies.
Inspect and analyze agent trajectories
When an AI agent does something unexpected, seeing its final response is often not enough. You need to understand what happened along the way.
The plugin records the agent trajectory and makes it available in two formats:
 HTML gives you a readable view of the agent’s messages, tool calls, and token usage.
 JSON makes trajectories available for programmatic analysis.
The JSON format is especially useful when you want to analyze multiple agent runs together, like to understand why an agent behaves a certain way or how to adjust the original prompt to get better results.
You can also use a local coding agent together with the TeamCity CLI to retrieve trajectories from multiple builds and analyze them in batches. This gives you a practical feedback loop: run an agent in CI, collect its trajectories, analyze what happened across multiple runs, adjust the prompt, and try again.
This makes trajectories useful both for debugging individual builds and improving the agent workflows you run in CI.
Set up the plugin
Install the plugin from JetBrains Marketplace and add it to your TeamCity server.
1. Create a connection 
First, you need to set up a connection. The plugin supports various LLM providers and gateways. Open Project Settings | Connections. 
Supported providers:
OpenAI
Anthropic
OpenRouter
LiteLLM
JetBrains Air




Enter the credentials required for your connection and save it.
If you’re using JetBrains Air, enter your service account client ID and client secret. Each team can use its own service account, which makes it possible to track shared AI usage and spending.
2. Add the AI Agent build feature
Open the build configuration where you want to use the coding agent and add the AI Agent build feature.
Select Codex or Claude Code, then select the provider connection.




3. Add your prompt
Add a Command Line build step and call codex or claude as usual. 
With Codex:
codex exec --ephemeral --skip-git-repo-check "summarize this repository"
With Claude Code:
claude -p "summarize this repository"
The plugin finds or installs the selected client and prepares its configuration for the build. You can replace these example prompts with whatever task you want the agent to perform as part of your build.




Review what the agent did
After the build finishes, the plugin publishes telemetry and agent trajectory files as hidden build artifacts under: .teamcity/ai-agents/.




It also publishes statistical values, such as prompt, completion, cached, and total token counts.




For a more convenient view, the plugin generates an HTML report showing the agent’s messages, tool calls, and token usage.




You can make this report available directly from the TeamCity build results. 
Go to Project Settings | Report Tabs, create a build report tab, and use: .teamcity/ai-agents/trajectory.html as the start page and “AI Agent Trajectory” as the name. This gives you a tab where you can inspect what the agent did during the build.




A note about sensitive data
The generated artifacts may contain prompts, source code, and model output. Treat them the same way you would other sensitive build artifacts and make sure access is appropriately restricted.
Try the plugin
The plugin is currently experimental, and its functionality may change as we continue developing it.
You can install it from JetBrains Marketplace and try running Codex or Claude Code in your TeamCity builds.
Install the plugin
We’d love to hear how you’re using it and what you’d like us to improve. Share your feedback in the TeamCity Slack community.

posts.title: AI models hate Python and love PHP: we asked 12 of them 1,200 times
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
1,200 hot takes, 14 “random” languages, zero opinions about C#, and one model that argued both sides of Go’s error handling.
We asked 12 AI models for their most controversial opinion about programming languages, 1,200 times in total.
We wanted to check one thing. When you give a model permission to be spicy, does it have a take of its own, or does it grab the same one as everybody else? Developers argue about languages for sport, so there should be plenty of takes to go around.
We picked 12 of the newest models, from ten labs in three countries:

LabModelsBased in

OpenAIGPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra, GPT-6 AstraUS
AnthropicClaude Opus 5.5US
GoogleGemini 4 ArgonUS
xAIGrok 4.7US
MetaMuse Spark OpenUS
DeepSeekDeepSeek V4 ProChina
AlibabaQwen3.8 2.4T A95BChina
Moonshot AIKimi K3.1 ProChina
Z.aiGLM 5.3China
Mistral AIMistral Large 4France





Each model got two questions, 50 times each, always in a fresh conversation with no system prompt:
“Choose one programming language at random. What is your most controversial hot take about that language?”
“What is your most controversial hot take about programming languages?”
Both prompts also asked for a one-sentence take, two or three sentences of reasoning, and 50 to 90 words. All 1,200 requests came back. Collecting them cost USD 7.68, about two-thirds of a cent per hot take. Opinions are cheap. We have receipts.

Only two ever defended it.", "sub": "Takes about Python in each model's 100 answers, both questions together. Attacks point left, defenses point right.", "lName": "attacks", "rName": "defenses", "lColor": "--rv-neg", "rColor": "--rv-pos", "rowHead": "model", "rows": [{"name": "Muse Spark Open", "l": 57, "r": 0, "m": 0}, {"name": "Gemini 4 Argon", "l": 55, "r": 0, "m": 0}, {"name": "Kimi K3.1 Pro", "l": 36, "r": 0, "m": 0}, {"name": "GPT-6 Astra", "l": 28, "r": 0, "m": 0}, {"name": "Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B", "l": 25, "r": 0, "m": 0}, {"name": "GPT-6.1 Sol", "l": 23, "r": 0, "m": 0}, {"name": "Grok 4.7", "l": 20, "r": 3, "m": 0}, {"name": "Mistral Large 4", "l": 19, "r": 0, "m": 0}, {"name": "GPT-6.1 Terra", "l": 17, "r": 0, "m": 0}, {"name": "Claude Opus 5.5", "l": 10, "r": 0, "m": 0}, {"name": "GLM 5.3", "l": 8, "r": 9, "m": 1, "tip": "One of those defenses: the GIL was the single best design decision Python ever made."}, {"name": "DeepSeek V4 Pro", "l": 1, "r": 0, "m": 0}], "caption": "Python got 312 takes: 299 attacks, 12 defenses and 1 mixed. Muse Spark Open and Gemini 4 Argon account for 112 of the attacks on their own. GLM 5.3 is the only model that defended Python more often than it attacked it, 9 to 8, and one of those defenses calls the GIL the best design decision the language ever made."} });
if (window.__RTKVIZ) window.__RTKVIZ.drain();





Ask for a random language, get Go or Python

The punching bags: Python, Rust and TypeScript
600 of those 904 attacks landed on three languages.
Python got 312 takes, and 299 of them were attacks. Every model went after it at least once, and ten of the twelve never said one nice thing about it in 100 tries. The exceptions were GLM 5.3 (9 defenses) and Grok 4.7 (3). Here is a typical attack, followed by what GLM counts as a defense:
Muse Spark Open
Python should have died a decade ago and is holding the industry back.
GLM 5.3
Python’s Global Interpreter Lock was the single best design decision the language ever made.
Gemini 4 Argon complained about significant whitespace 11 times.
Rust got 167 takes, and 164 were attacks. The most widely shared opinion in the whole experiment is about Rust: the ownership model costs more than it’s worth for ordinary application code. 78 takes from 9 of the 10 labs said so. Anthropic was the only lab that didn’t.
Grok 4.7
Rust’s borrow checker is a tax most programs should refuse to pay.
TypeScript got 138 takes and 137 attacks. Among languages with more than ten takes, none is attacked this consistently. It gets hit from both sides: 57 takes say its type safety costs more than it’s worth, and 24 say the safety is fake and gives you false confidence about what happens at runtime. Mistral Large 4 fit both complaints into one sentence:
Mistral Large 4
TypeScript is a productivity tax that JavaScript developers pay for the illusion of safety.
The single defense came from GPT-6.1 Sol, and it was really a dig at Python: TypeScript’s type system is “more valuable than Python’s readability for most production backends”.
Asked to pick a language at random, the models chose TypeScript 7 times out of 600. Asked an open question, they went after it 131 times. Nobody lands on TypeScript by chance, but everybody has something to say about it. GPT-6.1 Terra spent 43 of its 50 open answers attacking it.

The ones they love: PHP, Java and the old stuff
PHP got 28 takes, and all 28 were defenses. Claude Opus 5.5 and Kimi K3.1 Pro wrote 11 each, usually arguing that PHP’s throw-everything-away-after-each-request model beats a long-running Node.js or Python server.
Kimi K3.1 Pro
PHP is a better default than Python for most small business websites, and dismissing it as obsolete is snobbery, not engineering judgment.
Java got 90 takes and 80 defenses, mostly of checked exceptions (67 takes stand up for them). Claude Opus 5.5 opened 7 answers with “Java’s checked exceptions were a good idea, and the industry was wrong to abandon them.” GLM 5.3 wrote the identical sentence 3 more times. Two labs, one sentence, word for word.
The small numbers tell the same story. SQL got 5 defenses out of 5. Lisp got 3 out of 3, all from DeepSeek. Perl got its 1 out of 1 from Claude Opus 5.5, which also picked Lua 4 times and defended its 1-based indexing every time:
Claude Opus 5.5
Lua’s 1-based indexing is the correct design, and programmers who mock it are defending a habit rather than a principle.
DeepSeek V4 Pro
Lisp’s parentheses are genuinely an advantage, not a quirk.
The models’ “unpopular praise” is predictable: pick an old language people used to make fun of, then explain why it was right all along.

Go got 238 takes: 118 attacks, 118 defenses and 2 mixed. An exact tie, and most of the fighting is about if err != nil.
94 takes defend Go’s explicit error handling. 65 attack it, for five different reasons: it’s boilerplate that buries the logic (29), Go should have had exceptions (17), errors are too easy to ignore (8), it should borrow Rust’s ? operator (6), and real failures get lost in the noise (5).

The bills vary just as much. GPT-6 Astra’s 100 takes cost USD 1.27. DeepSeek’s 100 cost USD 0.03.
So, do they disagree?
A little. They disagree about Go’s error handling, and now and then they disagree with themselves. The rest reads like one long group chat. Python is a bad first language (35 takes from 8 labs). Rust’s borrow checker isn’t worth it for normal apps (9 labs). TypeScript is overhead. PHP and Java were secretly fine all along. One argument shape came up in all 10 labs: some simpler approach you already have makes the extra safety machinery redundant.
If your plan is to ask a few different models for fresh perspectives, don’t expect much variety. Expect the same takes in different fonts, plus some bold text from Claude.
How we did it (the boring part)
Show the boring part

Every answer came from a fresh, single-turn API call with no system prompt and each provider’s default settings. The 1,200 requests ran in shuffled order, and we kept every answer, boring ones included. Nothing was retried because we didn’t like it.
Two models, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, labeled every answer separately with the model names hidden. They recorded which language it targets, whether it attacks or defends, and which specific claim it makes. Gemini 4 Argon settled the disagreements. The two labelers agreed on the target 99% of the time and on the specific claim 94% of the time.
Yes, two of the labelers are also contestants. That’s why the names were hidden. A human pass over the headline groups is still on our list.
“Random” is an instruction we gave, not a sampling method anyone can verify. With 50 answers per model per question, we can see strong habits but not small differences.
DeepSeek and Qwen ran through third-party hosts (DeepInfra and Together) rather than their labs’ own APIs.
Quotes are verbatim. The only edit is straightened quote marks.

      lb.style.maxWidth = p.cssW + "px";
      lb.innerHTML = "" + r.name + "" + (r.aside ? " " + r.aside + "" : "");
      plot.append(lb);
      const yc = ys[i] + barTop + barH / 2;
      if (r.l + r.r === 0) {
        const nt = document.createElement("div"); nt.className = "rv-note";
        nt.style.top = yc + "px";
        nt.style.left = (axis * p.px + 8) + "px";
        nt.textContent = spec.zeroNote || "none";
        plot.append(nt);
        return;
      }
      const nl = document.createElement("div"); nl.className = "rv-num" + (r.l ? "" : " rv-zero");
      nl.style.top = yc + "px";
      nl.style.right = (p.cssW - (axis - wOf(r.l)) * p.px + 6) + "px";
      nl.textContent = fmtN(r.l);
      const nr = document.createElement("div"); nr.className = "rv-num" + (r.r ? "" : " rv-zero");
      nr.style.top = yc + "px";
      nr.style.left = ((axis + 1 + wOf(r.r)) * p.px + 6) + "px";
      nr.textContent = fmtN(r.r);
      plot.append(nl, nr);
    });
    const rowAt = (my) => ys.findIndex((y) => (my >= y ? my  {
      const rc = plot.getBoundingClientRect();
      const mx = e.clientX - rc.left, my = e.clientY - rc.top;
      const i = rowAt(my);
      const h = i ${fmtN(r.m)}
` : "";
      const extra = r.tip ? `
${r.tip}
` : "";
      tip.show(`
${r.name}
${spec.lName} ${fmtN(r.l)}
${spec.rName} ${fmtN(r.r)}
${mixed}${extra}`, mx, my);
    });
    plot.addEventListener("mouseleave", () => { hoverI = null; st.dirty = true; tip.hide(); });
    plot.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
      const rc = plot.getBoundingClientRect();
      const i = rowAt(e.clientY - rc.top);
      selected = i  r.m) || (spec.extraRows || []).length > 0;
    dataTable(el, [spec.rowHead || "row", spec.lName, spec.rName].concat(hasM ? ["mixed"] : []),
      rows.map((r) => [r.name, fmtN(r.l), fmtN(r.r)].concat(hasM ? [fmtN(r.m || 0)] : []))
        .concat(spec.extraRows || []));
  };

  /* meters: stat tiles, each with a dithered fill meter for "x of n" */
  RENDER.meters = function (el, spec) {
    header(el, spec);
    const grid = document.createElement("div"); grid.className = "rv-mtiles"; el.append(grid);
    const made = spec.tiles.map((t) => {
      const d = document.createElement("div"); d.className = "rv-mtile";
      const ph = document.createElement("div"); ph.className = "m-phrase"; ph.textContent = t.phrase;
      const who = document.createElement("div"); who.className = "m-who"; who.textContent = t.who;
      const val = document.createElement("div"); val.className = "m-val"; val.textContent = fmtN(t.value);
      const of = document.createElement("span"); of.className = "m-of"; of.textContent = "of " + fmtN(t.of) + " " + (t.ofLabel || "answers");
      val.append(of);
      const pl = document.createElement("div"); pl.className = "rv-plot";
      const det = document.createElement("div"); det.className = "m-detail"; det.textContent = t.detail || "";
      d.append(ph, who, val, pl, det);
      grid.append(d);
      return { t, pl };
    });
    const stops = [];
    made.forEach((m) => {
      const p = new DitherPlot(m.pl, el, { cssH: 12 });
      runLoop(el, p, (st) => {
        p.clear();
        p.barH(0, p.W, 0, p.H, p.color("--rv-grid"), { flat: 0.55 });
        p.barH(0, Math.max(p.W * m.t.value / m.t.of * st.reveal, 1), 0, p.H, p.color(spec.color || "--rv-c1"),
          { intensity: st.intensity });
        p.flush();
      }, { duration: 1100 });
      stops.push(el.__rvCleanup);
    });
    el.__rvCleanup = () => stops.forEach((f) => f());
    caption(el, spec);
    dataTable(el, ["phrase or habit", "model", "answers", "out of"],
      spec.tiles.map((t) => [t.phrase, t.who, fmtN(t.value), fmtN(t.of)]));
  };

  /* ptable: a tile board. Filled tiles carry a dithered level (area recipe,
     square-root scale) for how much they got; dashed ghost tiles got nothing.
     One canvas under the whole board, painted at each tile's laid-out rect. */
  RENDER.ptable = function (el, spec) {
    header(el, spec);
    const wrap = document.createElement("div"); wrap.className = "rv-plot rv-ptwrap"; el.append(wrap);
    const items = [];
    spec.groups.forEach((g) => {
      const h = document.createElement("div"); h.className = "rv-group"; h.textContent = g.label;
      const grid = document.createElement("div"); grid.className = "rv-ptable" + (g.ghost ? " rv-ptable-ghost" : "");
      g.tiles.forEach((t) => {
        const d = document.createElement("div");
        d.className = "rv-pt" + (g.ghost ? " rv-pt-ghost" : "") + (t.hot ? " rv-pt-hot" : "");
        if (!g.ghost) {
          const n = document.createElement("div"); n.className = "pt-n"; n.textContent = fmtN(t.value); d.append(n);
        }
        const nm = document.createElement("div"); nm.className = "pt-name"; nm.textContent = t.name; d.append(nm);
        if (t.note) {
          const nt = document.createElement("div"); nt.className = "pt-note"; nt.textContent = t.note; d.append(nt);
        }
        grid.append(d);
        items.push({ t, d, ghost: !!g.ghost });
      });
      wrap.append(h, grid);
    });
    const p = new DitherPlot(wrap, el, { cssH: wrap.offsetHeight });
    const maxV = Math.max(1, ...items.map((it) => (it.ghost ? 0 : it.t.value)));
    const w0 = wrap.getBoundingClientRect();
    items.forEach((it, i) => {
      const r = it.d.getBoundingClientRect();
      it.i = i;
      it.x0 = Math.round((r.left - w0.left) / CELL) + 2;
      it.x1 = Math.round((r.right - w0.left) / CELL) - 2;
      it.floor = Math.round((r.bottom - w0.top) / CELL) - 2;
      it.room = Math.round(r.height * (spec.fillMax || 0.42) / CELL);
      it.level = it.ghost ? 0 : Math.max(0.08, Math.sqrt(it.t.value / maxV));
    });
    let hov = null;

    function paint(st) {
      p.clear();
      items.forEach((it) => {
        if (it.ghost) return;
        const color = p.color(it.t.color || "--rv-neutral");
        const top = it.floor - it.room * it.level * clamp01(st.reveal * 1.4 - it.i * 0.025);
        const lift = hov === it ? 1 : st.intensity;
        for (let x = it.x0; x  0.3) {
          if (!REDUCED) {
            const tw = (Math.sin((st.tick + it.i * 47) * 0.35) + 1) / 2;
            if (tw > 0.85) {
              const a = (tw - 0.85) / 0.15;
              const sx = it.x0 + Math.round((it.x1 - it.x0) * (0.3 + 0.04 * ((it.i * 37) % 10)));
              const sy = Math.round(top + (it.floor - top) * 0.55);
              p.solid(sx, sy, 1, 1, color, a);
              p.solid(sx - 1, sy, 1, 1, color, a * 0.6);
              p.solid(sx + 1, sy, 1, 1, color, a * 0.6);
              p.solid(sx, sy - 1, 1, 1, color, a * 0.6);
              p.solid(sx, sy + 1, 1, 1, color, a * 0.6);
            }
          }
        }
      });
      p.flush();
    }
    const st = runLoop(el, p, paint, { wink: true, duration: 1300 });

    const tip = tooltip(wrap);
    items.forEach((it) => {
      it.d.addEventListener("mouseenter", () => { hov = it; st.dirty = true; });
      it.d.addEventListener("mouseleave", () => { hov = null; st.dirty = true; tip.hide(); });
      it.d.addEventListener("mousemove", (e) => {
        const rc = wrap.getBoundingClientRect();
        const t = it.t;
        const body = it.ghost
          ? `
takes aimed at it 0
answers naming it ${fmtN(t.ment)}
`
          : `
takes aimed at it ${fmtN(t.value)}
attacks ${fmtN(t.a)}
defenses ${fmtN(t.d)}
`;
        tip.show(`
${t.name}
${body}`, e.clientX - rc.left, e.clientY - rc.top);
      });
    });
    caption(el, spec);
    dataTable(el, spec.tableHead, spec.table);
  };


  /* ---------- mount / drain / re-render ---------- */
  const REGISTRY = new Map();  // id -> {type, spec}

  function mount(item) {
    const els = document.querySelectorAll('.rtkviz[id="' + item.id + '"]');
    if (!els.length) return false;
    if (els.length > 1) console.warn("rtkviz: duplicate widget id '" + item.id + "' — rendering every copy");
    REGISTRY.set(item.id, item);
    els.forEach(el => render(el, item));
    return true;
  }
  function render(el, item) {
    if (el.__rvCleanup) { el.__rvCleanup(); delete el.__rvCleanup; }
    el.innerHTML = "";
    try { (RENDER[item.type] || (() => {}))(el, item.spec); }
    catch (err) { el.textContent = "chart failed to render: " + err.message; }
  }
  function rerenderAll() {
    for (const [id, item] of REGISTRY) {
      document.querySelectorAll('.rtkviz[id="' + id + '"]').forEach(el => render(el, item));
    }
  }
  let rerenderTimer = null;
  const queueRerender = () => { clearTimeout(rerenderTimer); rerenderTimer = setTimeout(rerenderAll, 150); };

  window.__RTKVIZ = {
    drain() {
      const q = window.__RTKVIZ_Q || [];
      const rest = [];
      for (const item of q) if (!mount(item)) rest.push(item);
      window.__RTKVIZ_Q = rest;
    },
    rerender: rerenderAll,
  };

  const start = () => window.__RTKVIZ.drain();
  if (document.readyState === "loading") document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", start);
  else start();

  /* theme + resize reactivity */
  const darkMQ = matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)");
  if (darkMQ.addEventListener) darkMQ.addEventListener("change", queueRerender);
  new MutationObserver(queueRerender).observe(document.documentElement,
    { attributes: true, attributeFilter: ["data-rtkviz-theme"] });
  let lastW = window.innerWidth;
  window.addEventListener("resize", () => {
    if (Math.abs(window.innerWidth - lastW) > 40) { lastW = window.innerWidth; queueRerender(); }
  });
})();
